body.text: Tarkabhāṣā
body.translated_text: <s>Tarkabhāṣā</s> (Discourse on Logic)

body.text:
pratyakṣam
maṅgalācaraṇam
body.translated_text:
<s>Pratyakṣa</s> (Perception)
Auspicious invocation (<s>maṅgalācaraṇa</s>)

children.translated_text: Having bowed to the teacher, the Lord of the world, for the sake of children of dull intellect,
the <s>Tarkabhāṣā</s>, [following] the doctrine of <s>Dharmakīrti</s>, is set forth for [their] instruction.

body.text: pramāṇasāmānyalakṣaṇam
body.translated_text: General definition of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge)

body.text: iha khalu prekṣāpūrvakāriṇo 'rthijanāḥ sarvapuruṣārthasiddhinimittaṃ pramāṇamanusarantīti pramāṇamādau vyutpādyate / pramāṇaṃ samyagjñānamapūrvagocaram / pramīyate 'rtho 'neneti pramāṇam / tadeva samyagjñānam, sandehaviparyāsadoṣarahitatvāt / avisaṃvādakaṃ jñānaṃ loke samyag jñānamabhidhīyate / na ca saṃśayaviparyāsajñānayoravisaṃvādakatvamasti / yathā sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti jñānasya, marīcikāsu vā jalajñānasya / apūrvo gocaro asyetyapūrvagocaram / gocaro viṣayo ghaṭādiḥ / tasmādutpannaṃ tadarthaprāpaṇayogyaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇam // pramāṇasya kāryam
body.translated_text: Here indeed, those who desire objects and act with deliberation follow <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for the attainment of all human goals — therefore <s>pramāṇa</s> is explained first. <s>Pramāṇa</s> is correct knowledge (<s>samyagjñāna</s>) having a novel object (<s>apūrvagocara</s>). That by which an object is cognized (<s>pramīyate</s>) is <s>pramāṇa</s>. That itself is correct knowledge, because it is free from the faults of doubt and error. Non-deceiving knowledge is called 'correct knowledge' in the world. And there is no non-deceptiveness in knowledge that is doubtful or erroneous — as in the case of the knowledge 'Is it a post or a person?', or the knowledge of water in mirages. 'Having a novel object' means its object is unprecedented. The object (<s>gocara</s>) is the domain, such as a pot, etc. Knowledge arisen from that [object], capable of leading to the attainment of that object, is <s>pramāṇa</s>. // The function of <s>pramāṇa</s>

body.text: nanu jñānaṃ kartṛ puruṣaṃ prayojyamartha karmabhūtaṃ yadi kadācinna prāpayati tatkathamaprāpakatvāt pramāṇaṃ syāt? ucyate / na hi jñānena puruṣo gale pādukānyāyena balādarthe pravartayitavyaḥ / api tvevaṃbhūtamidaṃ vatusvarūpaṃ nānyathetyanenākāreṇa niścayo janayitavyaḥ / sa cettena kṛtaḥ, etāvataivāsya prāmāṇyamaviruddham / puruṣastu tatra prayojanavaśāt pravartatāmṛte prayojanaṃ na pravartatām, artho vā yogipiśācādibhirapahriyatām / jñānasya kimāyātam? // kṣaṇikaṃ sannapi pramāṇasya saṃgatiḥ
body.translated_text: Objection: If knowledge, [though] having the person as its agent and the object as that which is to be acted upon, sometimes does not lead [the person] to the object, then how can it be <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it does not lead [to the object]? Reply: Knowledge does not forcibly engage a person toward the object, like the maxim of shoes tied around the neck. Rather, the certainty of this form — 'This is the real nature of the thing, not otherwise' — is to be generated by it. And if that [certainty] has been produced by it, to that extent its validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) is unimpaired. Let the person engage there due to a purpose, or not engage if there is no purpose. Or let the object be taken away by <s>yogins</s>, demons, etc. — what is that to knowledge? // Compatibility of <s>pramāṇa</s> despite being momentary

body.text: nanvavisaṃvādakatvena jñānasya prāmāṇyam / avisaṃvādakatvaṃ ca dṛṣṭārthaprāpaṇāt / na ca yad dṛṣṭaṃ tatprāpyate, kṣaṇikatvāt kiṃ ca, rūpaṃ dṛṣṭa, prāpyate ca spraṣṭavyam / tato 'nyad dṛṣṭamanyat prāpyata ityapratītaprāpaṇāt kathaṃ prāmāṇyamasya saṃgacchatām / na, yadi nāma vastuto 'nyadeva prāpyate tathāpi dṛṣṭameva mayā prāptamityekatvādhyavasāyāt pratītaprāpaṇamabhidhīyate / yattu marīcikādijalajñānaṃ tadaprāpaṇayogyatvādapramāṇameva //
body.translated_text: Objection: The validity of knowledge consists in its non-deceptiveness. And non-deceptiveness [consists in] leading to the attainment of the perceived object. But what is perceived is not [the same thing as what is] attained, due to momentariness. Moreover, form is perceived, but what is attained is the tangible. Thus, something different is perceived and something different is attained — how can its validity hold, since it leads to the attainment of something not cognized? Reply: No — even though in reality something different is attained, still, because of the determination of identity — 'What I perceived is what I have attained' — it is said to lead to the attainment of what was cognized. The water-knowledge in mirages, etc., however, is indeed not <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it is incapable of leading to attainment.

body.text: arthakriyāsthitiḥ
body.translated_text: The establishment of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsthiti</s>)

body.text: nanvidaṃ prāpaṇayogyamidaṃ netyarthakriyā prāptimantareṇa niścetumaśakyam / jñānotpattimātreṇa tu na bhrāntābhrāntayorbhedo 'vadhāryate / tataśca kathaṃ tatsamyagjñānamiti cet? naiṣa doṣaḥ / yaddyapi jñānamātrodayād vaiśiṣṭyamanayoravadhārayituṃ na śakyate, tathāpi jñānaviśeṣodayāddyathaikasya vaiśiṣṭayaṃ tathocyate / tathā hi - yadi nāma mandabuddhirutpattivaśādavisaṃvādakatvaṃ jñānasya nāvadhārayituṃ samarthaḥ, tathāpi dāhapākāvagāhanasnānapānonmajjanāddyarthakriyāṃ dūrato 'nubhavato narasya darśanenoccalad dhūmādidarśanena cāvadhārayati / amandabuddhistu paṭutarapratyakṣeṇaivāvadhārayati, na tvarthakriyāprāptyā /
body.translated_text: Objection: Without actually experiencing causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>), one cannot determine 'this can lead to attainment, this cannot.' By the mere arising of knowledge, the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cannot be ascertained. How then can it be correct knowledge? Reply: This is no fault. Although the distinction between them cannot be ascertained from the mere arising of knowledge, still, from the arising of a particular kind of knowledge, the distinction is stated. For even a person of dull intellect, though unable to ascertain the non-deceptiveness of knowledge merely from its arising, still ascertains it from observing a person experiencing causal efficacy from afar — through burning, cooking, immersion, bathing, drinking, diving, etc. — and from seeing rising smoke, etc. But a person of keen intellect ascertains it by sharper perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) alone, not through [experiencing] causal efficacy.

body.text: yadyavisaṃvādalakṣaṇaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ tadā śrotrajñānasyādhigatārthāprāpakatvāt kathaṃ prāmāṇyamini cet? na / arthasvarūpapratītirhi prāmāṇyam / tacca bāhyārthakriyāprāptimantareṇāpi sambhavati / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: Objection: If validity consists in non-deceptiveness, then how does auditory knowledge have validity, since it does not lead to attainment of the cognized object? Reply: No — the cognition of the object's own nature is itself validity. And this is possible even without attainment of external causal efficacy. As it is said —

body.text: pramāṇamavisaṃvādi jñānamarthakriyāsthitiḥ /
body.translated_text: '<s>Pramāṇa</s> is non-deceiving knowledge; causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsthiti</s>) is its establishment.'

body.text: avisaṃvādanam iti /
body.translated_text: 'Non-deceiving' — thus [it is explained].

body.text: śabdasya śrutimātreṇaiva caritārthatvāt śrutireva tatrārthakriyāsthitiḥ / yathā ravicandrāmbudacitrādīnāṃ darśanamevārthakriyāsthitiḥ / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Since verbal knowledge achieves its purpose by mere hearing alone, hearing itself is the establishment of causal efficacy therein — just as the mere seeing of the sun, moon, clouds, paintings, etc. is itself the establishment of causal efficacy. As it is said —

body.text: jñeyasvarūpasaṃvittiriṣṭā tatra kriyāsthitiḥ iti /
body.translated_text: 'The cognition of the own-nature of the knowable is accepted as the establishment of [causal] efficacy therein.'

body.text: prathamaṃ tu prekṣāvānarthakriyārthitayā jalānalādāvarthakriyāsandehādeva pravartate /
body.translated_text: First, however, a discerning person acts out of desire for causal efficacy, precisely because of doubt about the causal efficacy of water, fire, etc.

body.text: yadi nāma tasyaiva nāsti sandeho me vartata iti tathāpi sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvādyuktaḥ sandeho bhavan kena vāryate iti / tasmāt
body.translated_text: Even if one says 'I have no doubt about this,' still, in the absence of establishing or refuting <s>pramāṇas</s>, what prevents a doubt that is rational from arising? Therefore —

body.text: sthitametat- āsāditanirantarārthakriyāvyavahārāt paṭutarapratyakṣodayādevārtha pravartate, mandabuddhistu tādrūpyānumānāditi /
body.translated_text: This is established: one acts either because of having encountered uninterrupted causal efficacy in practice, or from the arising of sharper perception; a person of dull intellect, however, [acts] from inference of that kind.

body.text: ata eva tu pratyakṣasya svataḥ prāmāṇyam / kasyacittu parataḥ / yogijñānasya svasaṃvedanasya ca svata eva prāmāṇyam / anumānasya tu niścayātmakatvāt svata eva pramāṇyam /
body.translated_text: For this very reason, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) has intrinsic validity (<s>svataḥ prāmāṇya</s>). For some, however, [validity is] extrinsic. <s>Yogic</s> knowledge and self-cognition (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) have intrinsic validity. Inference (<s>anumāna</s>), however, has intrinsic validity because it is of the nature of certainty.

body.text: apūrvagocaram
body.translated_text: Novel object (<s>apūrvagocara</s>)

body.text: tenāyamarthaḥ- prathamata eva yadvijñānaṃ viṣaye pravṛttaṃ tadeva pramāṇam, na tu tatraiva paścādbhāvi jñānāntaramapi, gṛhitagrāhitvena tasyāprāmāṇyāt / yathā ghaṭaṃ nirvikalpakena jñānena dṛṣṭvā paścāttasminneva viṣaye ghaṭo 'yamiti savikalpakaṃ jñānaṃ smaraṇarūpam, yathā vā parvatādau dhūmaṃ dṛṣṭvā vahniratretyanumānajñānānantaraṃ punarapi tatraiva vahniratretyanumānajñānam /
body.translated_text: The meaning is this: the very first cognition that arises regarding an object is <s>pramāṇa</s>, but not a subsequent cognition arising with respect to that same [object], because it grasps what has already been grasped and therefore lacks validity. For example, after perceiving a pot with non-conceptual knowledge (<s>nirvikalpaka jñāna</s>), the subsequent conceptual knowledge 'This is a pot' directed at that same object is of the nature of memory (<s>smaraṇa</s>). Likewise, after seeing smoke on a mountain, etc. and generating the inferential knowledge 'There is fire here,' a repeated inferential knowledge 'There is fire here' directed at the same [object is not pramāṇa].

body.text: indriyādera apramāṇam
body.translated_text: Sense organs, etc. are not <s>pramāṇa</s>

body.text: samyagjñānaṃ pramāṇamityukte sāmarthyājjaḍasvabhāvasyendriyādeḥ paricchedakatvābhāvāt prāmāṇyaṃ nirastam paricchedakatvaṃ hi boddhṛtvam / tacca jñānasyaiva nijarūpam / tatkathamajñānātmana indriyādeḥ svarūpaṃ bhavitumarhatīti //
body.translated_text: When it is said '<s>Pramāṇa</s> is correct knowledge,' by implication the validity of sense organs, etc., which are of an inert nature, is excluded, because they lack the capacity for determination (<s>paricchedakatva</s>). For the capacity for determination is awareness (<s>boddhṛtva</s>). And that is the very own nature of knowledge alone. How then could it be the nature of sense organs, etc., which are not of the nature of knowledge?

body.text: pramāṇasya dvaividhyam, pratyakṣaśabdanirvacanaṃ ca
body.translated_text: The twofold nature of <s>pramāṇa</s>, and the etymology of '<s>pratyakṣa</s>'

body.text: tad dvividhaṃ pratyakṣamanumānaṃ ceti / pratigatamakṣaṃ pratyakṣam / akṣamindriyaṃ cakṣuḥ śrotraghrāṇajihvākāyākhyam / tasmādutpannaṃ jñānaṃ pratyakṣamabhidhīyate / nanu yadyakṣāśritaṃ jñānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ tadā mānasādi vakṣyamāṇaṃ jñānatrayamindriyādanutpatteḥ pratyakṣaṃ na syāt? atrocyate- pratigatamakṣamiti yaduktaṃ tatpratyakṣaśabdasyāvyutpattimātranimittaṃ pratipāditam / pravṛttinimittaṃ tu pratyakṣaśabdasāyārthasākṣātkāritvameva ruḍhivaśādavagantavyaṃ paṅkajavat / tataḥ svasaṃvedanādikamapi jñānaṃ svasaṃvedanarūpamartha sākṣātkarotīti pratyakṣaśabdavācyaṃ siddhyatīti //
body.translated_text: That [<s>pramāṇa</s>] is twofold: <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference). <s>Pratyakṣa</s> [etymologically means] 'that which has reached (<s>pratigata</s>) the sense organ (<s>akṣa</s>).' The sense organ (<s>akṣa</s>) is the <s>indriya</s> (faculty), called eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. Knowledge arisen from that is called <s>pratyakṣa</s>. Objection: If knowledge based on a sense organ is <s>pratyakṣa</s>, then the three [other] kinds of knowledge to be discussed — mental perception, etc. — would not be <s>pratyakṣa</s>, since they do not arise from a sense organ? Reply: What was stated — 'that which has reached the sense organ' — is presented merely as the etymological derivation of the word <s>pratyakṣa</s>. But the ground for its application is the direct apprehension of the object (<s>arthasākṣātkāritva</s>), to be understood through conventional usage (<s>rūḍhi</s>), like <s>paṅkaja</s> ('mud-born,' i.e. lotus). Thus self-cognition (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) too, which directly apprehends its object in the form of self-awareness, is established as denoted by the word <s>pratyakṣa</s>.

body.text: anumānaśabdanirvacanam
body.translated_text: Etymology of '<s>anumāna</s>'

body.text: mīyate 'rtho 'neneti mānam / anuḥ paścādarthe / paścānmānamanumānam / liṅgagrahaṇaliṅgaliṅgisambandhasmaraṇayoḥ paścāt yadvijñānaṃ parvatādau dharmiṇi parokṣavastvālambakaṃ tadevānumānaśabdenābhidhīyate / etacca ruḍhivaśādavagantavyam /
body.translated_text: That by which an object is measured (<s>mīyate</s>) is <s>māna</s> (measurement/knowledge). <s>Anu</s> means 'after' in the sense of subsequence. <s>Anumāna</s> is knowledge that comes after. After the apprehension of the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and the recollection of the connection between the mark and the marked (<s>liṅgaliṅgisambandha</s>), the cognition that apprehends an imperceptible object on the subject (<s>dharmin</s>) such as a mountain, etc. — that alone is denoted by the word <s>anumāna</s>. And this [meaning] too is to be understood through conventional usage.

body.text: pramāṇasaṃkhyāvipratipattiḥ
body.translated_text: Disagreements about the number of <s>pramāṇas</s>

body.text:
dvividhavacanena ekaṃ trīṇi catvāri pañca ṣaḍhiti vipratipattayo nirasyante /
tathā hi pratyakṣamevaikaṃ pramāṇamiti cārvākaḥ / pratyakṣamanumānaṃ śābdaṃ ceti sāṃkhyaḥ /
body.translated_text:
By the statement 'twofold,' the rival positions [asserting] one, three, four, five, or six [pramāṇas] are refuted.
Thus: the <s>Cārvāka</s> [holds] that <s>pratyakṣa</s> alone is the one <s>pramāṇa</s>. The <s>Sāṃkhya</s> [holds]: <s>pratyakṣa</s>, <s>anumāna</s>, and <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony).

body.text: pratyakṣamanumānamupamānaṃ śābdaṃ ceti naiyāyikaḥ / pratyakṣamanumānaṃ śābdamupamānamarthapattiriti prābhākaraḥ / pratyakṣamanumānaṃ śābdamupamānamarthapattirabhāvaśceti mīmāṃsakaḥ /
body.translated_text: The <s>Naiyāyika</s> [holds]: <s>pratyakṣa</s>, <s>anumāna</s>, <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), and <s>śabda</s>. The <s>Prābhākara</s> [holds these four plus] <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). The <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> [holds these five plus] <s>abhāva</s> (absence).

body.text: dvividhavacanena dvitve prāpte pratyakṣamanumānaṃ ceti punaryaduktaṃ tadanyathādvitvanirāsārtham / tathā hi vaiyāka raṇo brūte pratyakṣaṃ śābdaṃ ceti pramāṇadvayam //
body.translated_text: Having established twoness by the statement 'twofold,' the reiteration 'perception and inference' serves to refute other [proposed] dyads. Thus, the Grammarian says: <s>pratyakṣa</s> and <s>śabda</s> are the two <s>pramāṇas</s>.

body.text: cārvākābhimatānumānāpramāṇyanirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of the <s>Cārvāka</s> view that inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is not valid

body.text:
tatra anumānasya prāmāṇyamavaśyamabhyupagantavyaṃ cārvākeṇeti pratipādyate /
tathā hi - sa khalu pratyakṣalakṣaṇaṃ parapratipādanāya praṇayati / parasya ca buddhirna pratyakṣā / kiṃ tarhi kāyavāgvyāpārādikāryādanumeyā / tato 'nena kāryaliṅgajamanumānaṃ balādabhyupagataṃ syāt / paralokaniṣedhāya cānupalambhākhyaṃ sādhanamācaṣṭe / ato 'sau svayamevānumānena pramāṇena vyavaharati, nānumānaṃ pramāṇamiti ca bruvan kathaṃ nāma nonmattaścārvākaḥ syāt?
body.translated_text:
It is demonstrated that the <s>Cārvāka</s> must necessarily accept the validity of inference.
For: he formulates the definition of <s>pratyakṣa</s> in order to communicate it to others. But another's cognition is not perceptible. Rather, it is to be inferred from effects such as bodily and verbal behavior. Thus, inference based on effects (<s>kāryaliṅgaja anumāna</s>) has been tacitly accepted by him. Furthermore, he employs the proof called 'non-apprehension' (<s>anupalambha</s>) to deny the afterlife. Thus he himself uses inference as a <s>pramāṇa</s> while saying 'inference is not <s>pramāṇa</s>' — how could such a <s>Cārvāka</s> not be considered mad?

body.text: śabdopamānārthāpatyabhāvānāṃ pramāṇāntaratvanirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of [the view that] verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>), analogy (<s>upamāna</s>), presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>), and absence (<s>abhāva</s>) are separate <s>pramāṇas</s>

body.text: śābdaṃ ca jñānaṃ bāhyārthāvisaṃvādakatvena pramāṇameṣṭavyam / avisaṃvādakatvaṃ ca sambandhamantareṇa na saṃgacchate / na ca śabdānāṃ bāhyārthena saha kaścitsambandho 'sti / tathā hi - śabdārthayoḥ sambandho bhavan tādātmyaṃ tadutpattirarvā bhavet / tatra na tāvāttādātmyaṃ śabdārthayoḥ, atyantabhedena pratibhāsanāt / tādātmyaṃ hyekatvamabhidhīyate bhinnapratibhāsayorapyekatve svīkriyamāṇe gavāśvādīnāmapyekatvaprasaṅgaḥ / nāpi tadutpattiḥ / nāpi tadutpattiḥ, anvayavyatirekābhāvāt / tasmāt tadutpattirityevaṃ vaktuṃ na śakyate / tathā hi - śabdavyāpāramantareṇa svahetoreva mṛtpiṇḍadaṇḍasalilakulālacakrādeḥ sakāśādutpadyamāno ghaṭādirartho dṛśyate / śabdo 'pi bāhyārtha vinaiva puruṣecchāmātreṇa tālvādivyāpārādevotpadyate /
body.translated_text: And verbal knowledge (<s>śābda jñāna</s>) must be accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) by virtue of its non-discordance with external objects. But non-discordance is not possible without a relation (<s>sambandha</s>). And there is no relation whatsoever between words and external objects. For the relation between word and meaning, if it exists, would be either identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) or causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>). First, there is no identity between word and meaning, since they appear as entirely distinct. For identity means oneness; if oneness were accepted even for things that appear as different, then the absurd consequence would follow that a cow and a horse, etc., are also identical. Nor is there causal origination [between them]. Nor is there causal origination, because of the absence of co-presence and co-absence (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>). Therefore, it cannot be said that there is causal origination. For it is observed that an object such as a pot arises from its own causes — a lump of clay, a stick, water, a potter’s wheel, etc. — without any operation of words. And a word too arises from the operation of the palate and other [speech organs] merely through the person’s desire, without any external object.

body.text: atha tādātmyatadutpattibhyāmanya eva vācyāvācakatvalakṣaṇaḥ śabdārthayoḥ vāstavaḥ sambandhadho 'sti / evaṃ tarhyasaṃketavido 'pi puruṣasya śabdāduccaritānniyatārthapratītiḥ prāptā, yogyatā mātreṇaiva pradīpāt ghaṭādipratītivat na caitadasti /
body.translated_text: But [if one says:] there is a real relation between word and meaning, distinct from identity and causal origination, characterized by the signified-signifier [relationship] — then in that case, even a person unfamiliar with the convention should, upon hearing a word uttered, obtain a cognition of a determinate meaning, merely by [the word’s] capacity, just as one cognizes a pot, etc., from a lamp. But this is not the case.

body.text: tathā hi - abhinavo nālikeradvīpādāyātaḥ pumānagniśabdaṃ śrutvāpyagniśabdānna kiñcidartha pratyetīti / atha tāṃstān saṃketānapekṣya tattadarthapratyāyanayogya evāyaṃ śabdo jāyata ityucyate / tanna / na hyevamasya prāmāṇyamavatiṣṭhate / sarvatra saṃketasya yogyatvāt / tato na jñāyate kiṃ vivakṣitārthamāha, āhosvidanyaṃ veti /
body.translated_text: For a newly arrived man from the Coconut Island (<s>Nālikeradvipā</s>), even upon hearing the word "fire" (<s>agniśabda</s>), understands nothing from the word "fire." But [if one says:] the word is produced as inherently capable of conveying such-and-such a meaning, depending on particular conventions — that is wrong. For in this way its validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) does not hold, since any convention could serve as the capacity. Therefore, one cannot know whether [the speaker] stated the intended meaning or something else.

body.text: astu vā anya eva kaścitsambandhaḥ / tathā ca so 'pi kena sambandhena tayoḥ sambaddha iti praṣṭavyaḥ / anyena caturthena sambandheneti cet, caturtho 'pi teṣu kena sambandhena sambaddhaḥ? pañcamena kenaciccet, so 'pi kenetyanavasthāyāṃ antyāsiddhau pūrveṣāmapyasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: Or let there be some other relation [between word and meaning]. Even so, by what relation is that [relation] connected to those two? If by yet a fourth relation, then by what relation is the fourth connected to them? If by some fifth, then by what is that [connected]? — and so on, in an infinite regress. When the last is unestablished, the preceding ones are also unestablished.

body.text: athāsambaddha eva śabdārthayoḥ samvandha iti cet / tanna / yo na sambaddhaḥ sa kathaṃ sambandho bhavati ghaṭasyeva paṭaḥ / atha vaktavyaṃ sambandhasya tādṛśa eva svabhāvaḥ, yena sambandhāntaranirapekṣa evaṃ paraṃ sambadhnāti? taduyuktam / pramāṇasiddhe hi svabhāve nottaramabhidhīyate / yathāgnerevāyamīdṛśaḥ svabhāvo yaduta dāhakatvaṃ nāma nānyasyākāśādeḥ / sambandhasiddhau tu pramāṇaṃ kiñcinnirupayanto na paśyāmaḥ / na caivaṃ vaktavyaṃ śabdaśaktisvabhāvādeva śabdānāṃ niyatārthāvyabhicāritvamiti / tathā hi - yadi ghaṭa ityayaṃ śabdaḥ svabhāvādeva kambugrīvākāraṃ vārisaṃdhāraṇasamartha padārthamabhidadhāti, tatkathaṃ saṃketāntaramapekṣya puruṣecchayā turagādikamabhidadhyāt / na hi śālibījaṃ svahetoraṅkurajananasvabhāvamutpannaṃ saṃketāntamapekṣya gardabhaṃ janayituṃ samartha syāt / nāpyāptapraṇītaśabdānāṃ prāmāṇyamabhidhātumucitam / āptatvasyaiva niścetumaśakyatvāt / tathā hi - āptatvaṃ kṣiṇadoṣatvamucyate / kṣīṇadoṣatā ca paracittavṛttiḥ kācidabhidhīyate / paracittavṛttīnāṃ durlakṣyatvāt, kāyavāgvyāpārādikāryaliṅgasyānyathāpi vṛttidarśanāt / sarāgā api vītarāgā iva ceṣṭanta iti nyāyātkathamāptatvaṃ niścīyatāmiti / samvandhadūṣaṇena ca vaidikaśabdānāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ nirastamiti pṛthaṅnoktam / kathaṃ tarhi sarvo 'yamasandigdho laukiko vyavahāra iti cet / tathā tathā saṃketena vivakṣāvaśāditi na kācit kṣatiḥ / yathoktam 'vakturabhiprāyaṃ sūcayeyuḥ śabdā iti //
body.translated_text: But if [one says:] the relation of word and meaning is itself unrelated [to anything else] — that is wrong. How can what is not related be a relation? It would be like a cloth in relation to a pot [i.e., unrelated]. But [if one says:] such is the very nature of the relation that, without depending on another relation, it connects the two — that is not right. For when a nature is established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, no further [question] is raised. Just as this is the very nature of fire, namely the capacity to burn — and not of anything else, such as space. But we do not see any <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the relation [of word and meaning]. Nor should one say that words have an invariable non-deviation toward determinate meanings simply by virtue of the inherent power (<s>śakti</s>) of words. For if the word "pot" (<s>ghaṭa</s>) by its very nature denotes an object with a neck-shaped opening capable of holding water, then how could it, depending on another convention, denote a horse, etc., by the speaker’s wish? A rice-seed, produced as having the nature of generating a sprout from its own cause, would not be capable of producing a donkey by depending on another convention. Nor is it proper to assert the validity of words composed by trustworthy persons (<s>āpta</s>s), since trustworthiness itself (<s>āptatva</s>) cannot be ascertained. For trustworthiness is said to be the state of having destroyed [all] faults. But the destruction of faults is said to be a certain state of another’s mind. Since the states of another’s mind are difficult to discern, and since the inferential mark — behavior of body and speech — is observed to occur otherwise as well (for even those with passion behave as if free from passion, according to the maxim), how can trustworthiness be ascertained? By refuting the relation [of word and meaning], the validity of Vedic words is also rejected — hence this is not stated separately. But [if one asks:] how then does all this unambiguous worldly usage [function]? [We answer:] Through convention, in accordance with the speaker’s intention — there is no difficulty. As stated: "Words indicate the intention of the speaker."

body.text: naiyāyikasammatasyopamānapramāṇasya nirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, as accepted by the <s>Naiyāyika</s>s

body.text: naiyāyikasyopamānaprapañcaḥ / yaḥ pratipattā gāṃ jānāti na gavayam, sa ca apadiṣṭaḥ svāminā araṇyaṃ gatvā gavayamānayeti / sa ca gavayaśabdavācyamarthamajānāno vanecaramanyaṃ tajjñaṃ puruṣaṃ pṛṣṭavān, kīdṛśo gavaya iti / sa cāha yādṛśī gaustādṛśo gavaya iti / tasyāraṇyagatasya preṣyapuruṣasya atideśa vākyārthasmaraṇasahakāri gavayasārūpyajñānaṃ kartṛ ayamasau gavayaśabdavācyo 'rtha iti pratipattiṃ phalasvarūpāṃ janayatpramāṇam / etaccāyuktam / yatprāmāṇyaṃ nāma viṣayavattayāṃ vyāptam / na cāsya nipuṇamapi nirupayanto viṣayaṃ saṃpaśyāmaḥ / tathā hi - samākhyā nāma sambandhaḥ tasya viṣayo varṇyate / sa ca paramārthato nāsti / dṛśyatve tasyānupalambhena bādhā / adṛśyatve tasya sattāsādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ nekṣyate / kiṃ ca - sa hi sambandhaḥ sambadhibhyāṃ bhinno 'bhinno vā / yadā bhinnastadā tayoḥ sambandhaḥ kena sambandheneti vācyam /
body.translated_text: The <s>Naiyāyika</s>’s elaborate account of <s>upamāna</s>: A person who knows a cow but not a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is instructed by his master: "Go to the forest and bring a <s>gavaya</s>." Not knowing the meaning of the word "<s>gavaya</s>," he asks another knowledgeable person in the forest: "What does a <s>gavaya</s> look like?" That person says: "A <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow." For that servant who has gone to the forest, the cognition of the <s>gavaya</s>’s resemblance to the cow, aided by the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement, is the instrument [of knowledge]; and the cognition "This is the object denoted by the word ‘<s>gavaya</s>’" is the result — [and this is] the <s>pramāṇa</s>. This is incorrect. For what is called validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) is pervaded by having an object. Yet even upon careful examination, we do not see its object. For the naming relation (<s>samākhyā</s>) is said to be its object. But that does not ultimately exist. If it were visible, it would be refuted by non-perception. If it were invisible, no <s>pramāṇa</s> establishing its existence is seen. Moreover, is that relation different from or identical to the relata? If different, then by what relation are the two related? — this must be stated.

body.text: sambandhāntarakalpanāyāmanavasthā / athābhinnastadā sambandhināveva kevalau / na samākhyā nāma sambandhaḥ kaścit / atha sambaddhabuddhijanakatvaṃ sambandhaḥ / tanna yuktam / yataḥ sambaddhāvetāviti buddhiḥ svahetubalāt sambaddhavastudvayādapi sambhāvyamānā na sambandhāntaramākṣiptuṃ prabhavati //
body.translated_text: In postulating another relation, there is an infinite regress. If identical [with the relata], then there are merely the two relata by themselves, and there is no relation called "naming." But if [one says:] the relation is the capacity to produce the cognition of being related — that is not right. For the cognition "these two are related," being possible from its own causal force and from the two related things [themselves], is not able to require yet another relation.

body.text: mīmāṃsakasammatasyopamānapramāṇasya nirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, as described by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>s

body.text:
evaṃ mīmāṃsakopavarṇitasyāpi prāmāṇyaṃ nirākartavyam / tathā hi, sādṛśyaviśiṣṭaḥ piṇḍaḥ piṇḍaviśiṣṭaṃ vā sādṛśyamupamānasya viṣayastena varṇyate / na ca sadṛśavastuno 'tiriktaṃ sādṛśyaṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ śakyate, pramāṇenāpratītatvāt /
tathā hi - yadi sadṛśādatiriktaṃ sādṛśyaṃ dṛśyaṃ syāt tadā dṛśyānulambhagrastametat / athādṛśyaṃ tadā tatpratibaddhaliṅgābhāvāt anumānādapi kathaṃ tatsiddhiḥ / sādṛśyapratyayastu svahetostathotpannena sadṛśavastunāpi kriyamāṇo ghaṭata iti na tatpratyayādapi tatsiddhiryuktā / upamānādeva sādṛśyasiddhiriti cet? na / yataḥ pramāṇāntarasiddhayoreva sādṛśyapiṇḍaoyoryo viśeṣaṇaviṣeṣyabhāvastasyopamānaviṣayatvaṃ tena vādinā parikalddhapyate / tatkathaṃ sādṛśyamātrasyāpyupamānāt siddhiriti //
body.translated_text: Likewise, the validity of [<s>upamāna</s>] as described by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> must also be refuted. For the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> holds that the object of <s>upamāna</s> is either a particular (<s>piṇḍa</s>) qualified by resemblance, or resemblance qualified by a particular. But resemblance (<s>sādṛśya</s>) as something over and above similar things cannot be established, because it is not cognized by any <s>pramāṇa</s>. For if resemblance, as something over and above similar things, were visible, it would be consumed by non-perception [i.e., refuted by the fact that it is not perceived]. If it were invisible, then due to the absence of any inferential mark connected with it, how could it be established even through inference? And the cognition of resemblance, being produced by its own cause and being possible even through a similar object that has arisen in that manner, is compatible [with that explanation] — therefore its establishment from that cognition is also not warranted. [Objection:] "Resemblance is established from <s>upamāna</s> alone." No, because the qualifier-qualified relationship between resemblance and the particular, both of which are already established by other <s>pramāṇa</s>s, is what the proponent imagines to be the object of <s>upamāna</s>. How then can even mere resemblance be established through <s>upamāna</s>?

body.text: arthāpattipramāṇanirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) as a <s>pramāṇa</s>

body.text: arthāpatterapi prāmāṇyaṃ pṛthaṅnopapadyate / tathā hi pratyakṣādipratīto yo 'rthaḥ sa yena vinā nopapadyate tasyārthasya kalpanamarthāpattirityarthāpatterlakṣaṇam / atredaṃ cintyate - yo 'sau pramāṇadṛṣṭo 'rthaḥ, tasya yadi parikalpyamānena parokṣārthena saha kaścittādāmyalakṣaṇaḥ tadutpattilakṣaṇo va pratibandho 'sti tadā svabhāvaliṅgajā kāryaliṅgajā vāsau pratipattirityarthāpattiranumānameva / atha nāsti pratibandhaḥ, tadānīmarthāpattiḥ pramāṇameva na bhavati, asambandhāt ghaṭātpaṭapratītivaditi //
body.translated_text: The validity of <s>arthāpatti</s> also does not hold separately. For the definition of <s>arthāpatti</s> is: the postulation of a fact without which a fact known through perception and the like would be inexplicable. Here we consider: if the object known through a <s>pramāṇa</s> has some real connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) with the postulated imperceptible object — whether a connection of essential nature (<s>tādātmya</s>) or of causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>) — then that cognition is either born from a natural sign or from an effect-sign, and thus <s>arthāpatti</s> is nothing but inference (<s>anumāna</s>). If, on the other hand, there is no real connection, then <s>arthāpatti</s> is simply not a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all, because of the absence of a connection — like cognizing a cloth from a pot.

body.text: abhāvapramāṇanirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of <s>abhāva</s> (absence) as a <s>pramāṇa</s>

body.text:
abhāvasya svarūpameva tāvannopalabhāmahe, kuta eva tasya prāmāṇyaṃ bhaviṣyati /
tathā hi -
body.translated_text: We do not even apprehend the very nature of absence — how then will it have validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s>? For —

body.text: pratyakṣādipramāṇānāmanutpattirabhāvākhyaṃ pramāṇaṃ mīmāṃsakairabhidhīyate / tatra keyamanutpattiḥ? kiṃ prasajyavṛtyā pramāṇānutpattimātram? atha paryudāsavṛtyā vastvantaram? vastvantaramapi jaḍarūpaṃ, jñānarūpaṃ vā? jñānamapi kiṃ jñānamātram ekajñānasaṃsargivastuno jñānaṃ vā? tatra na tāvat prasajyarūpo 'bhāvo yujyate / tasya sarvaśaktiśūnyatvāt paricchedakatvaṃ vā kathaṃ bhavet? ata eva kenāpi na tatpratidyate / yadāha paṇḍitacakracūḍāmaṇiḥ- nābhāvaḥ kasyacitpratipattiḥ pratipattiheturvā /
body.translated_text: The non-arising of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid cognition) is called <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) as a <s>pramāṇa</s> by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>. Now, what is this non-arising? Is it merely the non-arising of a <s>pramāṇa</s> in the sense of simple negation (<s>prasajya-vṛtti</s>)? Or is it something else in the sense of implicative negation (<s>paryudāsa-vṛtti</s>)? If it is something else, is it of an insentient nature or of the nature of cognition? If cognition, is it mere cognition or the cognition of an object associated with a single cognition? Now, absence in the form of simple negation is not tenable, because being devoid of all capacity, how could it have the power of determination? For this very reason, no one accepts it. As the crest-jewel of the circle of scholars states: 'Absence is not the cognition of anything, nor the cause of cognition.'

body.text: tasyāpi kathaṃ pratipattiḥ iti /
body.translated_text: 'How then could there be cognition of it?'

body.text: nāpi jaḍarūpam, jaḍasya paricchedakatvābhāvāt / na hi jaḍarūpaṃ śakaṭādikaṃ ghaṭaṃ paricchinattīti kvāpi dṛṣṭaṃ śrutaṃ veti / nāpi jñānamātram, deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭasyāpi sumeruśaṃkhacakravartipiśācāderapi jñānamātrādabhāvapramāṇādabhāvaprasaṅgāt / athaikajñānasaṃsargibhūtalādivastujñānamabhāvo 'bhidhīyate tadā pratyakṣaviśeṣasyaivābhāvapramāṇanāmaka raṇānnāsmākaṃ kācid vipratipattiriti / sthitametat- pratyakṣamanumānaṃ ceta dvividhameva pramāṇamiti //
body.translated_text: Nor is it of an insentient nature, because what is insentient has no capacity for determination. For it is neither seen nor heard anywhere that an insentient thing like a cart determines a pot. Nor is it mere cognition, because even for things remote in space, time, and nature—such as <s>Sumeru</s>, conch shells, <s>Cakravartins</s>, and <s>piśācas</s> (goblins)—from mere cognition as the <s>pramāṇa</s> of absence, their non-existence would absurdly follow. If the cognition of an object such as the ground associated with a single cognition is called absence, then since it is merely a particular kind of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) named 'absence-<s>pramāṇa</s>,' there is no disagreement on our part. Thus it is established that <s>pramāṇa</s> is only twofold: <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference).

body.text: pratyakṣalakṣaṇam
body.translated_text: Definition of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception)

body.text: tatra pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍhamabhrāntam / pūrvoparamanusandhāya śabdasaṅkīrṇākārā pratītirjalpākārā vā kalpanā / yathā vijñapuruṣasya so 'yaṃ ghaṭa iti pratītiḥ / bālamūkatiryagādīnāmantarjalpākārā parāmarśarūpā vā pratītiḥ / tathā coktam - abhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsapratītiḥ kalpanā // iti //
body.translated_text: <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is that which is free from conceptual construction (<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>) and non-erroneous (<s>abhrānta</s>). In connection with the foregoing, cognition whose form is mixed with words—that is, whose form is like internal speech—is <s>kalpanā</s> (conceptual construction). For example, the cognition of a learned person: 'This is that same pot.' Or the cognition of infants, mutes, animals, and the like, whose form is like internal speech or of the nature of mental grasping. As stated: '<s>Kalpanā</s> (conceptual construction) is cognition whose appearance is fit for association with verbal expression.'

body.text: nanu bālamūkādīnāmantarjalpākāraṃ kalpanājñānamastīti kuto niścetavyamiti ceta, vikalpakāryādiṣṭāpādānaparihārāt / dṛṣṭaṃ cedaṃ kārya bālamūkādau, īptisatārthasvīkaraṇamanīpsitārthatyajanaṃ nāma / bālamūkādivijñānasya kalpanātva sūcanena bhattoktālocanājñānaṃ savikalpakamiti pratipāditaṃ bhavati / kiṃ punaḥ kāraṇaṃ kalpanāvibhramātmakaṃ ca jñānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ na syāditi ceta? na / arthasvarūpasākṣākāri hi jñānaṃ pratyakṣamiti sarvoṣāṃ prasiddham / na ca kalpanāvibhramāvartharūpaṃ sākṣātkartu samarthau / tathā hi - arthagrāhakaṃ jñānamarthasya kāryam / artho hi grāhyatvāt jñānasya kāraṇam / yathoktam -
body.translated_text: If one asks: how is it to be ascertained that infants, mutes, and the like have conceptual cognition in the form of internal speech? Because there is no avoidance of the inference from the effects of conceptual thought and similar signs. For this effect is observed in infants, mutes, and the like—namely, the acceptance of desired objects and the rejection of undesired objects. By indicating the conceptual nature of the cognition of infants, mutes, and the like, it is also established that the <s>ālocana-jñāna</s> (bare apprehension) described by <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> is determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>). If one asks: for what reason would cognition that is of the nature of conceptual construction and error not be <s>pratyakṣa</s>? No—for it is well-known to all that cognition which directly reveals the true nature of an object is <s>pratyakṣa</s>. And neither conceptual construction nor error is capable of directly revealing the nature of an object. For cognition that grasps an object is the effect of that object. The object, being what is to be grasped, is the cause of cognition. As stated:

body.text: bhinnakālaṃ kathaṃ grāhyamiti cet grāhyatāṃ viduḥ /
body.translated_text: 'If one asks: how can what belongs to a different time be grasped? Those who know say that graspability

body.text: hetutvameva yuktijñā jñānākārārpaṇakṣamam // iti //
body.translated_text: is indeed causality—the capacity to impart its form to cognition.'

body.text: kalpanājñānamarthamantareṇa vāsanāmātrādevopajāyamānaṃ kathamarthasya kāryaṃ syāt, arthena saha anvayavyatirekābhāvāt / na hi yadantareṇāpi yadbhavati tattasya kāryam, atiprasaṅgāt / yadi punaḥ kalpanājñānamarthādupajāyeta, tenāpi tadā ghaṭādirartho dṛśyeta / tataścāndhasyāpi rūpadarśanaprasaṅgaḥ, na cāsti / ata evoktam -
body.translated_text: Conceptual cognition, arising merely from latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) without the object, how could it be an effect of the object, since there is no co-presence and co-absence (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) with the object? For that which exists even without something else is not the effect of that something else, due to over-extension. If, however, conceptual cognition were to arise from the object, then external objects such as pots would be perceived by it. And then even a blind person would perceive forms—but this is not the case. Therefore it is stated:

body.text: śābdyāṃ buddhāvarthasya pratyakṣa iva pratibhāsābhāvād nāsti kalpanāyā arthasākṣātkāritvam iti //
body.translated_text: In verbal cognition, since there is no appearance of the object as in <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>kalpanā</s> (conceptual construction) does not directly apprehend the object.

body.text: etena yaduktaṃ pareṇaḥ
body.translated_text: By this, what has been stated by the opponent:

children.text: na so 'sti pratyayo loke yaḥ śabdānugamādṛte /
children.translated_text: 'There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words;

children.text: anuviddhamiva jñānaṃ sarva śabdena bhāsate // iti //
children.translated_text: All cognition appears as if pervaded by words'—

body.text: tannirastam / tathāhi - ghaṭe purovartini uccāryamāṇe tatsamīpavarti bhūtalādijñānamuccāraṇarahitamanubhūyata eva / na ca tathā tatra śabdānugato 'sti / na ca vikalpadvayaṃ sakṛditi nyāyāt //
body.translated_text: that is refuted. For when a pot in front is being named, the cognition of the ground near it is experienced without any verbal expression. And it is not the case that two conceptual cognitions occur simultaneously, according to logical principle.

body.text: bhrāntajñānam
body.translated_text: Erroneous cognition

body.text: bhrāntamapi jñānaṃ nārthasākṣātkāri / bhrāntaṃ hyarthakriyāsamarthae vastuni viparyastamucyate / arthakriyākṣamaṃ ca vastusvarūpaṃ deśakālākāraniyataṃ, tatkathaṃ viparītapratibhāsinā bhrāntena jñānena sākṣātkriyate / yadāha ācāryaḥ- 'timirāśubhramaṇanauyānasaṃkṣobhādyanāhitavibhramaṃ jñānaṃ pratyakṣam ' // iti //
body.translated_text: Erroneous cognition also does not directly apprehend the object's true nature. For erroneous cognition is said to be distorted regarding a real thing capable of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsamartha</s>). And the real nature of a thing capable of causal efficacy is determined by specific place, time, and form—how then could it be directly apprehended by erroneous cognition that presents it in a distorted manner? As the <s>Ācārya</s> (Teacher) states: 'Cognition free from error not produced by cataracts, rapid movement, being on a boat, agitation, and the like is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception).'

body.text: etena kāmalinaḥ śukle śaṃkhe pītapratibhāsi jñānaṃ, bhramādalātādau cakrādinirbhāsi jñānaṃ, gacchantyāṃ nāvi sthitasya caladavṛkṣādibhrāntijñānaṃ, gāḍhamarmaprahārahatasya jvalatstambhādipratibhāsi jñānaṃ ca, na pratyakṣamityuktaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text: By this it is stated that the following are not <s>pratyakṣa</s>: the cognition of a jaundiced person that presents a white conch as yellow; the cognition that presents a circle and the like in a whirling firebrand; the cognition of a person standing still on a moving boat that erroneously perceives trees and the like as moving; and the cognition of a person struck on a vital point that presents luminous pillars and the like.

body.text: nanu yadi nāma tajjñānaṃ na pratyakṣaṃ kathaṃ tato vastuprāptiriti cet? na tato vastuprāptiḥ / kiṃ tarhi, jñānāntarādeveti kecit /
body.translated_text: If one asks: even if that cognition is not <s>pratyakṣa</s>, how does one obtain the real object from it? There is no obtaining of the object from it. What then? Some say it is from another cognition entirely.

body.text: pratyakṣasya cāturvidhyam
body.translated_text: The fourfold nature of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception)

body.text: taccaturvidhaṃ- indriyajñānaṃ mānasaṃ svasaṃdanaṃ yogijñānaṃ ceti /
body.translated_text: That is of four kinds: sense cognition (<s>indriya-jñāna</s>), mental cognition (<s>mānasa</s>), self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>), and yogic cognition (<s>yogi-jñāna</s>).

body.text: indriyapratyakṣam
body.translated_text: Sense perception (<s>indriya-pratyakṣa</s>)

body.text: cakṣurādīndriyapañcakāśrayeṇotpadyamānaṃ bāhyarūpādipañcaviṣayālambanamindriyapratyakṣam / tatra cakṣurvijñānaṃ rūpaviṣayam / śrotravijñānaṃ ca śabdaviṣayam / ghrāṇavijñānaṃ gandhaviṣayam / jihvāvijñānaṃ rasaviṣayam / kāyavijñānaṃ sparśaviṣayam /
body.translated_text: That which arises based on the five sense organs beginning with the eye and has as its object the five external objects beginning with form is sense perception (<s>indriya-pratyakṣa</s>). There, visual cognition (<s>cakṣur-vijñāna</s>) has form as its object; auditory cognition (<s>śrotra-vijñāna</s>) has sound as its object; olfactory cognition (<s>ghrāṇa-vijñāna</s>) has smell as its object; gustatory cognition (<s>jihvā-vijñāna</s>) has taste as its object; tactile cognition (<s>kāya-vijñāna</s>) has touch as its object.

body.text: indriyapratyakṣasya vyapadeśaḥ
body.translated_text: The designation of sense perception (<s>indriya-pratyakṣa</s>)

body.text: indriyapratyakṣamiti vyapadeśasyāsādhāraṇakāraṇatvaṃ nimittam / yathā bherīśabdo yavāṅkara iti / idaṃ ca pratyakṣaṃ yatraiva svānurūpaṃ vikalpaṃ janayati tatraiva pramāṇam, sāṃvyāvahārika pramāṇādhikārāditi //
body.translated_text: The reason for the designation 'sense perception' is that the sense organ is the uncommon cause (<s>asādhāraṇa-kāraṇa</s>). Just as one speaks of 'the sound of the drum' or 'the barley sprout.' And this perception is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) only with respect to that particular conceptual cognition which it generates in accordance with itself, since the topic concerns <s>pramāṇa</s> in the conventional sense (<s>sāṃvyavahārika</s>).

body.text: mānasapratyakṣam
body.translated_text: Mental perception (<s>mānasa-pratyakṣa</s>)

body.text: svaviṣayānantaraviṣayasahakāriṇendriyajñānena samanantarapratyayena janitaṃ manovijñānaṃ mānasam / svaśabdenendriyajñānamabhimatam, svasya viṣayo bāhyo ghaṭādiḥ, svaviṣayasyānantaraḥ, svaviṣayānantaraḥ indriyajñānaviṣayādanyo ghaṭādirdvitīyakṣaṇaḥ / tena sahakāriṇā saha militvā, indriyajñānenopādānena samanantarapratyayasaṃjñakena yajjanitaṃ tanmānasaṃ pratyakṣamucyate / tato yaduktaṃ pareṇātraḥ 'gṛhītagrāhitvamandhabadhirādyabhāvo yogijñānasyāpi mānasatvaprasaṅgaḥ avyavahāritvaṃ ca' iti / tannirastam / tathā hi - dvitīyakṣaṇagrahaṇāt gṛhītagrāhitvasya nirāsaḥ / indriyajñānajanitaṃ hi mānasam / andhādīnāṃ rūpādiviṣayālambanakamindriyajñānameva nāsti, kutastajjanitaṃ mānasaṃ bhaviṣyati? ato nāstyandhabadhirādyabhāvadoṣaḥ / samanantarapratyayaviśeṣaṇena yogijñānasya mānasapratyakṣaprasaṅgo nirastaḥ / samanantarapratyayaśabdaḥ svasantānavartinyupādānajñāne ruḍhyā prasiddhaḥ / tato bhinnasantānavartiyogijñānamapekṣya pṛthagjanacittānāṃ samanantarapratyayavyapadeśo nāstīti / avyavahāritvaṃ punarasya dūṣaṇaṃ nopapadyate, sūkṣmakālabhāvitvena pṛthagjanairdurlakṣyatvāt / vyavahārāṅgetvena cānabhyupagamāt / āgamaprasiddhaṃ hi mānasapratyakṣam / na tvasya niścāyakaṃ kiñcidasti / yathoktaṃ bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: Mental cognition (<s>manovijñāna</s>) is that which is produced by the sense cognition (<s>indriya-jñāna</s>) as the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantara-pratyaya</s>), cooperating with the object immediately following the object of that [sense cognition]. 'Its own' (<s>sva</s>) refers to sense cognition; 'its own object' is the external object such as a pot; 'immediately following its own object' means the second moment of the object such as the pot, which is different from the object of sense cognition. By that [second-moment object] as the cooperating condition, and by the sense cognition as the productive cause designated as the immediately preceding condition, what is produced is called mental perception (<s>mānasa-pratyakṣa</s>). Therefore, what the opponent has stated here—'it grasps what has already been grasped, there would be absence of blindness and deafness, yogic cognition too would absurdly be mental, and it would have no practical utility'—is refuted. For: grasping what is already grasped is avoided because it grasps the second moment. Mental cognition is produced by sense cognition; since the blind and others lack sense cognition having form and similar objects as their basis, how could mental cognition produced by it arise? Therefore, there is no fault of absence of blindness, deafness, and the like. By the qualifier 'immediately preceding condition,' the absurd consequence of yogic cognition being mental perception is avoided. The term 'immediately preceding condition' is established by convention as referring to the productive cognition within one's own continuum (<s>svasantāna</s>). Therefore, with respect to yogic cognition belonging to a different continuum, ordinary beings' minds cannot be designated as immediately preceding conditions. The charge of having no practical utility is also not valid, because being of extremely brief duration, it is difficult for ordinary persons to discern. And because it is not accepted as being instrumental to conventional activity. For mental perception is established by scripture (<s>āgama</s>). But there is nothing that can ascertain it independently. As the <s>Bhagavān</s> has stated:

body.text: `dvābhyāṃ bhikṣavo rūpaṃ gṛhyate, cakṣuṣā tadākṛṣṭenamanasā ca' iti //
body.translated_text: 'Form is grasped by two means, O <s>bhikṣus</s>: by the eye and by the mind drawn by it.'

body.text: nanu ca vyavahārānupayuktamupadarśayituṃ kiṃ prayojanam, īdṛglakṣaṇayuktaṃ yadi mānasaṃ pratyakṣaṃ syāt, na kaściddoṣaḥ syādityāgamasyāpi viśuddhiranena pratipāditeti prayojanam //
body.translated_text: If one asks: what is the purpose of demonstrating something not useful in practical convention? The purpose is this: if mental perception possessing such characteristics exists, there would be no fault, and the purity of the scripture (<s>āgama</s>) is thereby established.

body.text: svasaṃvedanapratyakṣam
body.translated_text: Self-awareness perception (<s>svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa</s>)

body.text: cittacaittānāṃ svasaṃvedanatvasamarthanam
body.translated_text: Establishing the self-awareness of mind and mental factors (<s>citta-caitta</s>)

body.text: sarvacittacaittānāmātmasaṃvedanaṃ svasaṃvedanam / cittaṃ vastumātragrāhakaṃ jñānam / citte bhāvāḥ caittāḥ, vastuno viśeṣarūpagrāhakā sukhaduḥkhopakṣālakṣaṇāḥ / teṣāṃ sarvacittacaittānāmātmā saṃvidyate yena rūpeṇa tatsvarūpamātmasvarūpasākṣatkāritvāt svasaṃvedanaṃ pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍhamabhrāntaṃ cocyate /
body.translated_text: The self-cognition of all mind and mental factors (<s>citta-caitta</s>) is <s>svasaṃvedana</s> (self-awareness). Mind (<s>citta</s>) is cognition grasping the bare object. Mental factors (<s>caitta</s>) are states arising in mind that grasp the specific aspects of the object, characterized by pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), and equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). The self-awareness of all these mind and mental factors—that by which their own nature is cognized, directly apprehending their intrinsic nature—is called <s>svasaṃvedana pratyakṣa</s> (self-awareness perception), free from conceptual construction (<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>) and non-erroneous (<s>abhrānta</s>).

body.text: atra kecidāhuḥ - na ca cittacaittānāṃ svasaṃvedanaṃ ghaṭate, svātmani kriyāvirodhāt / na ca suśikṣito 'pi naṭavaṭuḥ svaskandhamāroḍhuṃ śaknoti / na hi tīkṣṇāpyasidhārā svamātmānaṃ chinatti / na hi prajjvalito 'pi vahniskandha ātmānaṃ dahati / tathā cittacaittamapi kathamātmānaṃ vedayatu vedyavedakabhāvo hi karmakartṛbhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here some say: Self-cognition (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) of mind (<s>citta</s>) and mental factors (<s>caittas</s>) is not tenable, because action upon oneself is contradictory. Even a well-trained acrobat boy cannot climb upon his own shoulders. A sword-blade, however sharp, does not cut its own self. A fire, however blazing, does not burn itself. Likewise, how can mind and mental factors cognize themselves? For the relation of the cognized and the cognizer is [in fact] the relation of object and agent.

body.text: karmakartṛtvaṃ ca loke bhedenaiva prasiddham, vṛkṣasūtradhārayoriva / atrocyate, na karmakartṛbhāvena vedyavedakatvaṃ jñāne varṇyate / kiṃ tarhi? vyavasthāpyavyavasthāpakabhāvena /
body.translated_text: And the agent-object relation is well-known in the world only as [involving] a distinction [between two things], like a tree and a thread-holder. To this we reply: The cognized-cognizer relation in knowledge is not described as an agent-object relation. Rather, it is described as the relation of the characterized and the characterizer (<s>vyavasthāpya-vyavasthāpaka</s>).

body.text: yathā pradipa ātmānaṃ prakāśayati tathā jñānamapi jaḍapadārthavilakṣaṇaṃ svahetoreva prakāśasvabhāvamupajāyamānaṃ svasaṃvedanaṃ vyavasthāpyate / tathā coktam -
body.translated_text: Just as a lamp illuminates itself, so too knowledge, being distinct from inert objects, arising from its own cause with the nature of luminosity, is established as self-cognition. And thus it has been said:

children.translated_text: Consciousness arises as distinguished from inert forms;
this very non-inertness of it is its self-awareness. //

body.text: alaṅkārakāreṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: The author of the <s>Alaṅkāra</s> (i.e., <s>Dharmakīrti</s>) has also said:

children.translated_text: The agent-object relation and the like are conceptually constructed; they do not exist in ultimate reality.
'The self destroys itself by itself' — thus it is etymologically explained. //

body.text: na ca cittacaittānāṃ jñānāntareṇa prakāśyatvaṃ yujyate / tathā hi - na tāvatsamānakālabhāvinā jñānāntareṇa cittacaittaṃ prakāśyata iti ghaṭate, upakāryopakārakatvābhāvāt, savyetaragoviṣāṇayoriva / nāpi bhinnakālabhāvinā, kṣaṇikatvāt, prakāśitavyasyaivābhāvāt / api ca yadi jñānaṃ svasaṃvedanaṃ na syāt, tadā jñāto 'rtho iti durghaṭaḥ syāt, 'nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇā buddhirviśeṣye varttate' iti nyāyāt / tathā hi - artho viśeṣyaḥ, jñāta iti viśeṣaṇam, jñāto jñānena viśeṣita iti / jñānaṃ cetsvayaṃ na bodharūpeṇa pratītaṃ, tatkathaṃ jñānena viśeṣito 'rthaḥ pratīyatām / na hi daṇḍāgrahaṇe daṇḍino grahaṇaṃ yuktisaṅgatam / yaccoktaṃ trilocanena -
body.translated_text: Nor is it tenable that mind and mental factors are illuminated by another cognition. For, first, it is not tenable that mind and mental factors are illuminated by another cognition existing at the same time, because there is no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary [between simultaneous cognitions], like the right and left horns of a cow. Nor [can they be illuminated] by one existing at a different time, because, [things being] momentary, the very thing to be illuminated would not exist. Moreover, if knowledge were not self-cognizing, then 'the object is known' would be untenable, according to the principle that 'a cognition does not operate upon the qualificand without having grasped the qualifier.' For: the object is the qualificand, 'known' is the qualifier, 'known by knowledge' means 'qualified by knowledge.' And if knowledge itself is not apprehended as having the nature of awareness, then how can the object as qualified by knowledge be apprehended? For without grasping the staff, it is not logically consistent to grasp the staff-bearer. And what <s>Trilocana</s> has said:

body.text:
cakṣuṣo 'grahaṇe 'pi cākṣuṣaṃ rūpaṃ pratīyate, tathā
jñānānavabodhe 'pi jñāto 'rtha iti ghaṭiṣyate // iti //
body.translated_text: 'Even without the eye being grasped, a visible form is apprehended; likewise, even without knowledge being cognized, "the object is known" will be tenable' —

body.text: tadasādhu / prastute 'nupayogāt / na hi cakṣū rūpasya viśeṣaṇam / kiṃ tarhi? cakṣurvijñānāsaṃvedane kathaṃ jñāyatāmiti codyamakṣatameva //
body.translated_text: that is not valid, because it is not useful in the matter at hand. For the eye is not a qualifier of form. Rather, [the objection stands:] how is it known if visual consciousness is not self-cognized? — this challenge remains unrefuted.

body.text: yatpunarjñānasya parokṣatvapratipādanāya bhaṭṭenoktam -
body.translated_text: Furthermore, what <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> (<s>Kumārila</s>) has said in order to establish that knowledge is indirect (<s>parokṣa</s>):

body.text: yathā ca rūpādiprakāśanyathānupapatyā indriyasiddhiḥ, tathā jñānasyāpi siddhiriti /
body.translated_text: 'Just as sense-faculties are established through the impossibility of explaining the illumination of form and the like in any other way, so too the existence of knowledge [is established]' —

body.text: tathā hi tatra bhāṣyam -
body.translated_text: and thus the <s>Bhāṣya</s> on that [states]:

body.text: na hi kaścidajñāte 'rthe buddhimupalabhate / jñāte tvanumānādavagacchati iti //
body.translated_text: 'For no one apprehends a cognition regarding an unknown object. But with regard to a known [object], one understands [that cognition occurred] through inference.' //

body.text: vārtikaṃ ca -
body.translated_text: And the <s>Vārttika</s> [states]:

body.text: tasya jñānaṃ tu jñātatāvaśāt / iti /
body.translated_text: 'The knowledge of that [cognition] is through the state of being known (<s>jñātatā</s>).' //

body.text: jñātatā ca viṣayaprākaṭyamucyate / tadapi cāyuktam / prākaṭyasyāpi jñānāt pṛthaktve viṣayarūpatāyāṃ vyaktau jaḍarūpatā, jaḍasya prakāśāyogāt / viṣayādarthāntaratve jaḍatāyāṃ tasyāpi svataḥ prakāśāyogāt / prākaṭayāntareṇa nu prakāśane 'navasthā syāt / jñānasvabhāvatve prākaṭayasyāpi parokṣatvaprasaṅgaḥ / tato 'vaśyaṃ jñānasya svasaṃvedanatvamabhidheyam / anubhavaprasiddhaṃ ca svasaṃvedanatva kathamapahnuyeta? taduktam - apratyakṣopalambhasya nārthadṛṣṭiḥ prasiddhayati / iti /
body.translated_text: And 'the state of being known' is said to be the manifestness of the object. But this too is untenable. If manifestness were different from knowledge and had the nature of an object, then when manifest, it would be inert — and what is inert cannot illuminate. If it were something other than the object, then being inert, it too could not illuminate by itself. If it were illuminated by another manifestness, there would be an infinite regress. If manifestness had the nature of knowledge, then manifestness too would be subject to the charge of being indirect. Therefore, self-cognition of knowledge must necessarily be affirmed. And how can self-cognition, which is well-established through experience, be denied? Thus it has been said: 'For one for whom apprehension is not directly perceived, the cognition of an object is not established.' //

body.text: alaṅkārakāro 'pyāha -
body.translated_text: The author of the <s>Alaṅkāra</s> also says:

children.text: parokṣaṃ yadi tat jñānaṃ jñātamityeva tatkutaḥ /
children.translated_text: If that knowledge were indirect, whence would 'it is known' [come]?

children.text: parokṣasya svarūpaṃ kastasya lakṣayituṃ kṣamaḥ // iti //
children.translated_text: Who is capable of ascertaining the own-nature of what is indirect? //

body.text: nanu sarvajñānānāṃ svasaṃvedanapratyakṣatve ghaṭo 'yamityādivikalpajñānasya nirvikalpakatvaṃ, pītaśaṅkhādijñānasyābhrāntatvaṃ ca kathaṃ na bhavet? ucyate - vikalpajñānamapi svātmani nirvikalpameva / ghaṭo 'yamityanena bāhyamevārtha vikalpayati, na tvātmānam / taduktam -
body.translated_text: Now, [objection:] if all cognitions are directly perceived through self-cognition, how would conceptual cognition such as 'this is a pot' not be non-conceptual? And how would cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like not be non-erroneous? We reply: Even conceptual cognition is non-conceptual with respect to itself. By 'this is a pot,' one conceptualizes only the external object, not one's own self. Thus it has been said:

children.translated_text: Where a cognition apprehends word-meanings, there it is conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>);
but the own-nature [of that cognition] is not a word-meaning; therefore, in that [respect], all [cognition] is direct perception. //

body.text: bhrāntamapyātmanyabhrāntaṃ svaprakāśarūpeṇaivāvabhāsanāt / asadviṣayatvācca bhrāntirucyate / taduktam - svarūpe sarvamabhrāntaṃ pararūpe viparyayaḥ / iti //
body.translated_text: Even erroneous [cognition] is non-erroneous with respect to itself, because it appears in its own self-luminous nature. It is called erroneous because of having a non-existent object. Thus it has been said: 'With respect to its own nature, everything is non-erroneous; with respect to another nature, there is error.' //

body.text: tasmādanyathā prakāśāsiddheḥ yadyamī prakāśante, tadā svahetoreva prakāśasvabhāvādutpannāḥ santaḥ prakāśanta iti svīkartavyam //
body.translated_text: Therefore, since illumination cannot be established in any other way, if these [cognitions] are luminous, then it must be accepted that they are luminous because, arising from their own causes, they arise with the very nature of luminosity.

body.text: yogipratyakṣanirūpaṇam
body.translated_text: Determination of Yogic Perception (<s>yogipratyakṣa</s>)

body.text: bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajaṃ yogijñānaṃ ceti / yogaḥ samādhiḥ, cittaikāgratālakṣaṇaḥ / niśśeṣavastutatvavivecikā prajñā / yogo 'syāstīti yogī / yogino yat jñānaṃ tatpratyakṣam / kīdṛśaṃ taditi cet? bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajam / bhūtārthaḥ pramāṇopapannārthaḥ / bhāvanā punaḥ punaścetasi samāropaḥ / bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantājjātaṃ yadvijñānaṃ tat kalpanāpoḍhabhrāntam / bhūtārthaścaturāryasatya duḥkhasamudayanirodhamārgasaṃjñakam, pañcaskandhasvabhāvaṃ kṣaṇikaśūnyanirātmakaduḥkhādirūpatayā pratipattavyam / yatsat tat kṣaṇikamityādyanumānena pramāṇopapannamupagantavyamiti //
body.translated_text: 'And the cognition of a yogin, born from the culmination of the cultivation of a real object' — <s>yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s> (meditative concentration), characterized by one-pointedness of mind. Wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) discriminates the reality of all things without remainder. One who has <s>yoga</s> is a <s>yogin</s>. The cognition of the <s>yogin</s> is direct perception. Of what kind is it? Born from the culmination of the cultivation of a real object. A 'real object' (<s>bhūtārtha</s>) is an object established by valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). 'Cultivation' (<s>bhāvanā</s>) is repeated mental application. The cognition that arises from the culmination of the cultivation of a real object is free from conceptual construction and error. The 'real object' is the four noble truths (<s>catvāry āryasatyāni</s>), designated as suffering, origin, cessation, and path, having the nature of the five aggregates (<s>pañcaskandha</s>), to be understood as being momentary, empty, selfless, suffering, and so forth. 'What is real is momentary' — this and the like should be accepted as established by inference through valid means of knowledge.

body.text: nanu bhāvanā vikalpaḥ, vikalpaścāvastuviṣayaḥ, tatkathaṃ vastunaḥ sphuṭībhāvo bhavatu /kathaṃ vā vikalpo nirvikalpatāṃ vrajet? kṣaṇikaṃ ca citaṃ kathamekāgrībhavati? viśeṣaśca kasya kena vā kriyatām? śarīrī ca rāgādivirahānmuktaśceti sarvamasaṃgatam / atrocyate - avastuviṣayo 'pi vikalpo vastvadhyavasyatīti bhāvanāto vastuna evātra sphuṭībhāvaḥ / na ca vikalpa eva nirvikalpakaḥ, kiṃ tu vikalpānnirvikalpakasyodayaḥ / anubhavasiddhaṃ caitat bhāvayatāṃ nirvikalpakapratibhāsanaṃ, kāmaśokādivat / na hi dṛṣṭe kiñcidanupapannaṃ nāma / kṣaṇikamapi cittaṃ sajātīyakṣaṇeṣu grahaṇapravīṇatvāt ekāgramucyate / kṣaṇikatvanaiva viśeṣotpattiḥ, na tu nityatvena, nityasyānādheyātiśayatvāt yaduktam -
body.translated_text: Now, [objection:] cultivation is conceptual; and conceptual thought has a non-real object. So how can there be a vivid apprehension of a real thing? And how can conceptual thought become non-conceptual? And [since] mind is momentary, how can it become one-pointed? And whose transformation is effected, and by what? And an embodied being, being liberated through the absence of passion and the like — all this is inconsistent. To this we reply: Even though conceptual thought has a non-real object, it determines a real thing — therefore through cultivation, there is indeed a vivid apprehension of the real thing. And it is not that conceptual thought itself becomes non-conceptual; rather, non-conceptual [cognition] arises from conceptual [thought]. And this is established through the experience of meditators — the arising of non-conceptual appearances, like desire, grief, and the like. For nothing that is directly observed is untenable. Even momentary mind is called one-pointed because of its proficiency in apprehending homogeneous moments. Transformation arises precisely because of momentariness, not because of permanence, since what is permanent cannot receive any additional excellence. As it has been said:

children.text: nityaṃ tamāhurvidvāṃso yaḥ svabhāvo na naśyati /
children.translated_text: The learned call that permanent which is a nature that does not perish;
its power or powerlessness, which is established by nature —

children.text: nityavādapi kiṃ tasya kastāṃ kṣapayituṃ kṣamaḥ // iti //
children.translated_text: even a proponent of permanence [must ask:] who is capable of removing that [nature] from it? //

body.text: yattu śarīritve sukhaduḥkhayorbhāvādanugrahanigrahāt śarīrī rāgādivirahānmukta śceti vighaṭanamuktaṃ, tadayuktam / na hi śarīraṃ rāgādihetuḥ, kiṃ tu avidyā / anitye nityamiti, anātmanyātmeti, duḥkhe sukhamiti, aśucau śuciteti, caturvipayāsasvabhāvā mithyopalabdhiḥ / ata eva viṣayasukhatṛṣṇā syāt / ātmānaṃ nityaṃ paśyata eva sukhābhikāṅkṣaṇādisukhaheturātmīyaḥ syāt / eṣu cā 'saṅgo rāgaḥ / etatpratibandhāśca dveṣādayaḥ / tasmādavidyaiva mūlaṃ rāgāderna tu śarīram / satyapi śarīre yadyavidyā na syāt, kuta eva rāgādiyogāḥ? tasmājjīvaccharīre satyapi avidyāvirahāt sarvasaṅgavirahalakṣaṇā muktirvītarāgāṇāṃ bhavatīti sarvaṃ susthitam /
body.translated_text: As for the objection that liberation of an embodied being through the absence of passion and the like is untenable because pleasure and pain exist as long as there is a body, and therefore [there must be] favor and disfavor — that is unjustified. For the body is not the cause of passion and the like; rather, it is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). [Ignorance is] the wrong apprehension having the nature of the four errors (<s>catuḥviparyāsa</s>): [apprehending] the impermanent as permanent, the selfless as self, suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure. From this very [ignorance], craving for the pleasures of objects arises. Seeing the self as permanent, there is desire for pleasure and the like — the cause of pleasure would be [something regarded as] one's own. Attachment to these is passion (<s>rāga</s>). And hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>) and the like are the obstructors of this [attachment]. Therefore, ignorance alone is the root of passion and the like, not the body. Even though the body exists, if ignorance did not exist, whence would the afflictions of passion and the like come? Therefore, even while the living body exists, through the absence of ignorance, liberation characterized by the absence of all attachment occurs for those who are free from passion — thus everything is well-established.

body.text: pratyakṣasya svalakṣaṇāviṣayatvasamarthanam
body.translated_text: Establishing that the Object of Direct Perception is the Particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>)

body.text: tasya viṣayaḥ svalakṣaṇam / tasya caturvidhasya pratyakṣasya svalakṣaṇaṃ viṣayo boddhavyaḥ / svalakṣaṇamityasādhāraṇaṃ vastusvarūpaṃ deśakālākāraniyatam / etenaitaduktaṃ bhavati- ghaṭādirudakādyāharaṇasamartho deśakālākāraniyataḥ puraḥ prakāśamāno 'nityatvādyanekadharmāntarodāsīnaḥ pravṛttiviṣayaḥ sajātīyavijātīyavyāvṛttaḥ svalakṣaṇamityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: Its object is the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>). The particular should be understood as the object of that fourfold direct perception. 'Particular' means the unique own-nature of a thing, determined by place, time, and form. By this, the following is stated: a pot and the like, capable of carrying water and the like, determined by place, time, and form, manifestly present, indifferent to the many other properties such as impermanence, the object of purposeful activity, distinguished from what is of the same class and what is of a different class — this is what is meant by 'particular.'

body.text: ayogānyogavyavacchedayoḥ bhedaḥ
body.translated_text: The Distinction between Exclusion of Inapplicability and Exclusion of Misapplicability

body.text: nanu yadi svalakṣaṇameva pratyakṣasya viṣayo na sāmānyaṃ tadānīṃ dhūmadahanasāmānyayorvyāptiḥ kathaṃ pratyakṣeṇa gṛhyatām? nāyaṃ doṣaḥ / yato 'yogavyavacchedena svalakṣaṇaṃ tasya viṣaya eva, na tvanyayogavyavacchedena svalakṣaṇameva tasya viṣaya iti / kiṃ tarhi, sāmānyamapyasya viṣayaḥ /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If only the particular (<s>svalākṣaṇa</s>) is the object of perception and not the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), then how can the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) between the universals of smoke and fire be grasped by perception? This is no fault. For the particular is its object by exclusion of the unfit (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>), but it is not the case that the particular alone is its object by exclusion of all other connection (<s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s>). Rather, the universal too is its object.

body.text: pramāṇa phala vyavasthā
body.translated_text: The determination of the <s>pramāṇa</s> and its result

body.text: dvividho hi pramāṇasya viṣayaḥ grāhyo 'dhyavaseyaśca / tatra pratyakṣasya pratibhāsamānaṃ svalakṣaṇam eko grāhyaḥ / adhyavaseyastu pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvino vikalpasya pratibhāsamānaṃ sāmānyameva / tacca sāmānyaṃ dvividham, ūrdhvatālakṣaṇaṃ tiryaglakṣaṇaṃ ceti / tatraikasyāmeva ghaṭādivyaktau sajātīyavyāvṛttāyāmanekakṣaṇasamudāyaḥ sāmānyaṃ ūrdhvatālakṣaṇaṃ sādhanapratyakṣasya viṣayaḥ / vijātīyavyāvṛttāstvanekavyaktayaḥ tiryaksāmānyaṃ vyāptigrāhakapratyakṣasya viṣayaḥ / anumānasya tu sāmānyaṃ grāhyaṃ, adhyavaseyastu svalakṣaṇameva / pratyakṣasya svalakṣaṇaviṣayapratipādane paroktāḥ ṣaṭ padārthā na viṣayā ityuktam yathā - avayavidravyaṃ, guṇaḥ, karma, sāmānyaṃ, viśeṣaḥ, samavāyaśceti / na caiṣāṃ pratyakṣe jñāne pratibhāso 'sti / na cāpratibhāsamāno viṣayo yujyate, atiprasaṅgāt / tathā hi - ghaṭādau paridṛśyamāne pūrvāparādibhāgaṃ vihāya nānyatkiñcidekamavayavidravyamupalabhāmahe / yadāha nyāyaparameśvaraḥ -
body.translated_text: The object of a <s>pramāṇa</s> is twofold: the grasped (<s>grāhya</s>) and the determined (<s>adhyavaseya</s>). Therein, one grasped [object] of perception is the particular (<s>svalākṣaṇa</s>) that appears [to it]. The determined [object], however, is the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) that appears to the conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) following upon perception. And that universal is twofold: vertical (<s>ūrdhvatālakṣaṇa</s>) and horizontal (<s>tiryaglakṣaṇa</s>). Therein, in a single instance of a pot, etc., distinguished from its own kind, the aggregate of many moments is the vertical universal — the object of establishing perception. But the many instances distinguished from different kinds constitute the horizontal universal — the object of the perception that grasps pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>). For inference, the grasped is the universal, while the determined is the particular alone. In demonstrating that the particular is the object of perception, it has been stated that the six categories affirmed by the opponent are not [its] objects, namely: the whole-possessing substance (<s>avayavidravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), action (<s>karma</s>), universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), ultimate differentiator (<s>viśeṣa</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). None of these appear in perceptual cognition. And what does not appear cannot reasonably be an object, due to over-extension. For when a pot and the like are being perceived, apart from the front, back, and other parts, we do not apprehend any single whole-possessing substance. As the supreme master of logic (<s>Nyāyaparameśvara</s>) has said:

children.text: bhāgā eva hi bhāsante sanniviṣṭāstathā tathā /
children.translated_text: "For only the parts appear, arranged in this or that way;
but the possessor of parts is never perceived as something distinct."

body.text: evaṃ guṇakarmādīnāṃ ca duṣaṇaṃ pratyetabyam //
body.translated_text: Likewise, the refutation of quality, action, and the rest should be understood.

body.text: pramāṇaphalāvabodhaḥ
body.translated_text: Understanding of the <s>pramāṇa</s>-result

body.text: nanu pramitirūpāṃ kriyāṃ phalabhūtāṃ niṣpādayajjñānaṃ pramāṇamiti prasiddham / tatra kāsau pramitiḥ, yāṃ janajjñānaṃ pramāṇamiti cet? ucyate - iha nīlāderarthāt jñānaṃ dvirūpamutpadyate nīlākāraṃ, nīlabodhasvabhāvaṃ ca / tatrānīlākāravyāvṛtyā nīlākāraṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇam / anīlabodhavyāvṛtyā nīlabodharūpaṃ pramitiḥ / saiva phalam / yathoktam -
body.translated_text: [Objection:] It is well-known that the cognition which produces an activity in the form of ascertainment (<s>pramiti</s>), which is the result, is the <s>pramāṇa</s>. What then is that ascertainment which, when produced, makes the cognition a <s>pramāṇa</s>? [Reply:] Here, from an object such as blue, a cognition arises with two aspects: having the form of blue, and having the nature of apprehending blue. Of these, the cognition having the form of blue, by exclusion of the non-blue-form, is the <s>pramāṇa</s>. By exclusion of non-blue-apprehension, the cognition in the form of blue-apprehension is the ascertainment (<s>pramiti</s>). That itself is the result (<s>phala</s>). As stated:

body.text: arthasārūpyamasya pramāṇam, arthādhigatiḥ pramāṇaphalam / iti //
body.translated_text: "The cognition's conformity with the object is the <s>pramāṇa</s>; the apprehension of the object is the <s>pramāṇa</s>-result."

body.text:
etacca vikalpapratyayena bhinnaṃ vyavasthāpyate paramārthatastu nāstyeva bhedaḥ /
yathoktam -
body.translated_text: This is distinguished by conceptual cognition, but ultimately (<s>paramārthatas</s>) there is no difference whatsoever. As stated:

body.text: tadeva pratyakṣaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaphalam / iti //
body.translated_text: "That very perceptual cognition is both <s>pramāṇa</s> and result."

body.text: pramāṇatatphalayorabhedaḥ
body.translated_text: The non-difference of <s>pramāṇa</s> and its result

body.text:
sākāraṃ cedaṃ jñānameṣṭavyam / yadi punaḥ sākāraṃ jñānaṃ neṣyate, tadānākāratvena sarvatra viṣaye tulyatvāt vibhāgena viṣayavyavasthā na sidhyati / yatpunaḥ kecidāhuḥ - pūrvaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ uttaraṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaphalamiti, tanna yuktam /
tathā hi prathamakṣaṇabhāvi tāvajjñānaṃ pramāṇaphalabhūtasya dvitīyajñānasyānutpatteḥ,phalabhūtajñānotpattau ca pūrvasya kṣaṇikatvena vināśāt kathaṃ ghaṭādiviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ bhavati? nāpi samānakālabhāvi jñānaṃ phalamucitam, upakāryopakārakatvābhāvāt, savyetaragoviṣāṇayoriva / [tasmāt paramārthataḥ pramāṇaphalayornāsti bhedaḥ / kālpanikastu vyāvṛttikṛto bhedaḥ vikalpabuddhau vyavasthāpyate] //
body.translated_text: This cognition must be accepted as having form (<s>sākāra</s>). If, however, cognition is not accepted as having form, then being formless, it would be identical with respect to all objects, and the determination of [different] objects through distinction would not be established. As for what some say — that the prior cognition is the <s>pramāṇa</s> and the subsequent cognition is the <s>pramāṇa</s>-result — that is not right. For the first-moment cognition [acts as <s>pramāṇa</s>] before the second cognition, which is the result, has arisen; and when the result-cognition arises, the prior [cognition] has perished due to its momentariness. How then can a cognition having a pot and the like as its object be a <s>pramāṇa</s>? Nor is a cognition existing simultaneously [with another] appropriate as a result, because of the absence of a helper-helped relationship — like the left and right horns of a cow. [Therefore, ultimately there is no difference between <s>pramāṇa</s> and result. But a constructed difference, produced by exclusion, is established in conceptual cognition.]

body.text: iti tarkabhāṣāyāṃ pratyakṣaparicchedaḥ prathamaḥ samāptaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the first chapter on <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) in the <s>Tarkabhāṣā</s>.

body.text: svārthānumānam
body.translated_text: Inference for oneself (<s>svārthānumāna</s>)

body.text: anumānasya dvaividhyam svārthānumānalakṣaṇam
body.translated_text: The twofold nature of inference; the definition of inference for oneself

body.text: anumānaṃ dvividham - svārthaṃ parārthaṃ ca / svasmai yattat svārthamanumānaṃ jñānātmakam / parvatādau dharmiṇi dhūmādikaṃ dṛṣṭvā yasya pratipattuḥ vahnijñānamutpadyate, sa eva tena jñānena parokṣamarthaṃ pratipadyate nānya iti svārthānumānamucyate / parasmai yattat parārtham / parārthānumānaṃ vacanātmakam / trirūpaliṅgapratipādakaṃ vacanaṃ paraṃ pratipādayati jñāpayatīti kṛtvā vacanamapyanumānaśabdenocyate, upacārāt, yathā āyurghṛtamiti /
body.translated_text: Inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is twofold: for oneself (<s>svārtha</s>) and for others (<s>parārtha</s>). That which is for oneself is inference for oneself — it is of the nature of cognition. When, having seen smoke and the like as a property of the subject (<s>dharmin</s>) such as a mountain, the cognition of fire arises in a cognizer — he alone, through that cognition, apprehends the imperceptible object, and no one else; hence it is called inference for oneself. That which is for others is inference for others — it is of the nature of verbal statement. A statement that demonstrates a sign (<s>liṅga</s>) possessing three characteristics communicates to and informs another; therefore the statement too is designated by the word "inference," by figurative usage, just as one says "ghee is life."

body.text: anumānasya kāryam
body.translated_text: The function of inference

body.text: tatra svārtha trirūpaliṅgādyadanumeye jñānam / rūpatrayayuktālliṅgādanumeye parokṣaviṣaye yad jñānaṃ rpatipatturutpadyate, tat svārthānumānam / tacca dharmaviśeṣa sambandhitayā sādhyāvinābhāvitvaniścaya ityeke /
body.translated_text: Therein, in inference for oneself, [the function is] the cognition [arising] from a sign possessing three characteristics regarding the object to be inferred. The cognition that arises in the cognizer regarding the imperceptible object to be inferred, from a sign possessing the three characteristics, is inference for oneself. Some say it is the ascertainment that [the sign] is invariably concomitant with the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved), being related as a particular property.

body.text: agnyadhyavasāya ityanye /
body.translated_text: Others say it is the determination of fire [or the <s>sādhya</s>].

body.text: liṅgasya trirūpatvam
body.translated_text: The three characteristics of the sign (<s>liṅga</s>)

body.text: samprati liṅgasya trirūpatvamucyate - anumeye satvameva niścitam / anumeye parvatādau dharmiṇi liṅgasyāstitvameva niścitaṃ, tadekaṃ rūpaṃ pakṣadharmatāsaṃjñakam / atra sattvagrahaṇenāsiddhasya nirāsaḥ, yathā - anityaśśabdaścākṣuṣatvāt, cākṣuṣatvaṃ cakṣurvijñānagrāhyatvamucyate, tacca śabde dharmiṇi nāsti / evakāreṇa pakṣaikadeśāsiddhasya nirāsaḥ, yathā digambaraprayogaḥ - cetanāstaravaḥ svāpāt / patrasaṅkocalakṣaṇo hi svāpaḥ, sa ca sarveṣu taruṣvasiddhaḥ / niścitagrahaṇena sandigdhāsiddhasya nirāsaḥ, yathā - agniratra vāṣpāditvena sandihyamānād bhūtasaṃghātāt / satvaśabdātpaścādevakāreṇa asādhāraṇasya nirāsaḥ, yathā- anityaśśabdaḥ śrāvaṇatvāt ghaṭavat //
body.translated_text: Now the three characteristics of the sign are stated: its ascertained presence in the subject (<s>anumeya</s>). The sign's ascertained existence in the subject such as a mountain — that is the first characteristic, designated as "being a property of the thesis" (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>). By the word "presence" (<s>sattva</s>), the unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>) is rejected, as in: "Sound is impermanent because it is visible" — visibility means being graspable by visual cognition, which does not exist in the subject, sound. By the word "only" (<s>eva</s>), the unestablished in one part of the thesis (<s>pakṣaikadesasiddha</s>) is rejected, as in the <s>Digambara</s>'s argument: "Trees are sentient because they sleep" — for sleep, characterized by leaf-folding, is not established in all trees. By the word "ascertained" (<s>niścita</s>), the doubtfully unestablished (<s>sandigdhāsiddha</s>) is rejected, as in: "There is fire here, from a mass of elements about which there is doubt as to whether it is steam or the like." By the word "only" after "presence," the uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>) is rejected, as in: "Sound is impermanent because it is audible, like a pot."

body.text: sapakṣanirūpaṇam
