For example: if the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is accepted as having manifold occurrence, the consequence of its being manifold. Thus: whatever has manifold occurrence is manifold, like a palm-fruit placed in many vessels. And the universal has manifold occurrence. Therefore, this [universal] too must be manifold — this is the <s>prasaṅga</s>.

body.text: prasaṅgasya kāryam
body.translated_text: The function of <s>prasaṅga</s>

body.text: athānekatvaṃ neṣyate, tadānekavṛttitvaṃ ca mā svīkurvīthāḥ /
body.translated_text: Now if you do not accept multiplicity, then do not accept manifold occurrence either!

body.text: nanu yadyetat prasaṅgākhyaṃ sādhanaṃ pramāṇa, na bhavati [trairūpyābhāvāt] kathamasyopanyāsa iti,
body.translated_text: Objection: If this proof called <s>prasaṅga</s> is not a [proper] <s>pramāṇa</s> [because it lacks the triple characterization], how can it be presented?

body.text: vyāptismaraṇārthaṃ vyāpyaikadeśakathanavaditi / yaduktam -
body.translated_text: [Reply:] Like stating part of the pervaded in order to recall the concomitance. As it has been said —

body.text: `prasaṅgo dvayasambandhādekābhāve 'nyahānaye' iti /
body.translated_text: '<s>Prasaṅga</s> [operates] from the connection of two [things]: when one is absent, the other is abandoned.'

body.text: asyāyamarthaḥ - vyāpyavyāpakayoḥ sambandhe sati yadi vyāpakaṃ neṣyate tadā vyāpyamapi neṣyatām / atha vyāpyamiṣyate tadā vyāpakamapīṣyatāmiti /
body.translated_text: The meaning of this is: when there is a connection between the pervaded and the pervader, if the pervader is not accepted, then the pervaded too should not be accepted. If the pervaded is accepted, then the pervader too should be accepted.

body.text: vādinā sādhanā upanyaste prativādinā tatra dūṣaṇaṃ vaktavyamiti nyāyaḥ /
body.translated_text: When the proponent presents a proof, the rule is that the opponent must state a refutation (<s>dūṣaṇa</s>) against it.

body.text: asiddhaviruddhānaikāntikānāmanyatamasyodbhāvanaṃ dūṣaṇam / yathoktam -
body.translated_text: Refutation (<s>dūṣaṇa</s>) is the demonstration that one of the three — unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), or inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) — [applies to the reason]. As it has been said —

body.text: `dūṣaṇāni nyūnatādyukti' iti /
body.translated_text: 'Refutations are statements of deficiency, etc.'

body.text: hetudūṣaṇam
body.translated_text: Refutation of the reason (<s>hetudūṣaṇa</s>)

body.text: nanveṣāmevodbhāvanaṃ yadi dūṣaṇaṃ,kva tarhi vaiyarthyāsāmarthyātiprasaṅgādīnāmantarbhāvaḥ? atraiva triṣu / tatra vaiyarthyaṃ tāvadasiddhe 'ntarbhavati / sandigdhasādhyadharmo hi heturucyate / vaiyarthyaṃ tu yatropanyasyate tatra sandigdhasādhyadharmakatvaṃ hetorlakṣaṇaṃ hetau na sambhavatīti asiddha ucyate / [hetorlakṣaṇasyāsiddheḥ] yaduktam -
body.translated_text: Now, if merely bringing these [fallacies] to light is the refutation, where then is the classification of futility (<s>vaiyārthya</s>), incapability (<s>asāmarthya</s>), overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>), and the like? In these very three [categories]. Among them, futility is subsumed under the unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>). For a reason whose property to be proved is in doubt is called [genuinely] a reason. But futility, where it is presented, means that the characteristic of a reason — namely, having the property to be proved as doubtful — does not apply to the reason, so it is called unestablished [because the characteristic of the reason is unestablished]. As it has been said:

body.text: `sandigdhe hetuvacanāt vyasto hetoranāśrayaḥ' iti /
body.translated_text: 'From the statement of a reason when [the probandum is already] doubtful, the opposite reason has no basis.'

body.text: asāmarthyaṃ tu svarūpāsiddhāvantarbhavati / na hi hetoḥ sāmarthya nāma hetusvarūpādanyat / hetoravastutvaprasaṅgāt / atiprasaṅgaścānaikāntike 'ntarbhāvyaḥ, sādhyadharmamatikramya vipakṣe 'pi prasakteriti //
body.translated_text: Incapability, however, is subsumed under non-establishment of own-nature (<s>svarūpāsiddhi</s>). For the capability of a reason is nothing other than the own-nature of the reason — because [otherwise] the reason would absurdly become a non-entity. Overextension is to be subsumed under the inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because it extends [its applicability] even to the dissimilar instance, transgressing the property to be proved.

body.text: ātmanirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of the Self (<s>Ātman</s>)

body.text: yatra tu dharmiṇi sādhyaṃ sādhayitumārabdhaṃ tasya dharmiṇaḥ pramāṇabādhitve āśrayāsiddhirhetordūṣaṇam / yathā sarvagata ātmā sarvatropalabhyamānaguṇatvāt / tadiha bauddhasyātmaiva na siddhaḥ, kiṃ punasasya sarvadeśopalabhyamānaguṇatvaṃ setsyati / tathā hi, tairthikāḥ khalvevaṃ bruvanti / śarīrādivastuvyatiriktaṃ śubhāśubhakarmakartṛtatphalabhoktṛ nityavyāpirūpamātmākhyaṃ dravyāntaramasti / tena ca yadi nāma viśvaṃ vyāptaṃ tadapi yadupabhogāyatanatayā pareṇa parigṛhītaṃ jīvaccharīraṃ tadeva sātmakamabhidhīyata iti / etaccāyuktam / ātmanaḥ siddhaye pramāṇābhāvāt / na hi pratyakṣeṇa ātmā pratīyate /
body.translated_text: But where one undertakes to prove a probandum with respect to a subject (<s>dharmin</s>), and that subject is invalidated by valid means of knowledge, non-establishment of the basis (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>) is the fault of the reason. For example: 'The self is omnipresent, because it has qualities apprehended everywhere.' Here, for the Buddhist, the self itself is not established — how then would its having qualities apprehended in all places be established? For the non-Buddhist philosophers (<s>tairthikas</s>) indeed say thus: there exists another substance called the self, distinct from the body and other things, the agent of good and evil actions, the experiencer of their fruits, eternal, pervasive in nature. And even if the entire [world] is pervaded by it, nevertheless only the living body, which is taken by another as the seat of experience, is called 'ensouled.' But this is unjustified, because there is no valid means of knowledge to establish the self. For the self is not apprehended through perception.

body.text: cakṣurādijñānānāṃ rūpādiviṣayapañcakaniyatatvāt / mānasasyāpyahaṃpratyayasya śarīrādiviṣayatvāt gauro 'haṃ sthūlo 'haṃ gacchāmyahamityādyākāreṇa ahaṃ pratyaya utpadyate yadāha alaṅkārakāraḥ -
body.translated_text: Because the cognitions of the eye and the other [senses] are restricted to the five types of objects beginning with form. And even the mental cognition of the 'I'-notion has the body and the like as its object — the 'I'-notion arises in the form 'I am fair,' 'I am stout,' 'I am going,' and so forth. As the author of the <s>Alaṅkāra</s> has said:

children.translated_text: That cognition which is 'I' perceives only a portion of the body and sense-faculties;
'I [am] one-eyed, happy, fair' — due to the awareness having a common basis [with the body]. //

body.text: na cāsya śarīravyatiriktasya taddharmo gauratvaṃ sthūlatvaṃ vā / na ca vibhoramūrttasya mūrtadravyānuvidhāyinī gamanakriyā yuktimatī / na cāyaṃ māṇavake siṃhapratyaya eva bhākto yuktaḥ, skhaladvṛttiprasaṅgāt / nāpyanumānena pratīyate, kāryasvabhāvaliṅgābhāvāt / nityaparokṣeṇa deśakālākāravyatirekavikalenātmanā saha kasyacidanvayavyatirekātmakāryakāraṇabhāvāsiddheḥ kāryaliṅgāyogat / dharmisattāyāścāsiddhatvāt svabhāvaliṅgānupapatteḥ / na cānyalliṅgamasti / anyenāpi liṅgena bhavatā sādhyavyāptena bhavitavyam / tasya ca sarvathāsiddheḥ, kathaṃ tena vyāptatvaṃ liṅgasya niścīyatām? kiñca, kiyamātmā bodharūpaḥ, abodharūpo vā? yadi bodharūpo nityaśca tadā cakṣurādivaiphalyaprasaṅgo durvāraḥ / athānityo bodharūpastadājñānasyaivātmeti nāma kṛtam, na vipratipattiḥ / athābodharūpo dṛśyaśca tadānupalambho 'sya sattāṃ na kṣamata iti nirātmasiddhiranavadyā / tasmāt sarvaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ vastu nirātmakamiti //
body.translated_text: Nor does fairness or stoutness belong to [something] distinct from the body. Nor is the action of going, which follows corporeal substance, logically consistent for [an ātman that is] all-pervading and incorporeal. Nor is this merely a figurative usage, like [calling] a boy a lion, because that would lead to a defective usage throughout [language]. Nor is [the self] apprehended through inference, because there is no mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of the effect-type or of the nature-type. Because the self is eternally imperceptible, lacking differentiation of place, time, and form, the causal relation of the effect-mark type — which requires positive and negative concomitance — is not established with any [putative self]; hence the effect-mark is inapplicable. And because the existence of the subject (<s>dharmin</s>) is unestablished, the nature-mark is untenable. Nor is there any other mark. Even another mark must be pervaded by the probandum. And since that [pervasion] is in no way established, how can the invariable connection of the mark [with the probandum] be ascertained? Furthermore, is this self of the nature of consciousness or not? If it is of the nature of consciousness and eternal, then the absurd consequence that the eye and the other [senses] would be useless is unavoidable. If it is of the nature of consciousness but impermanent, then it is merely cognition given the name 'self' — there is no disagreement [with the Buddhist view]. But if it is not of the nature of consciousness and is perceptible, then its non-apprehension does not tolerate its existence — thus the proof of selflessness is unimpeachable. Therefore, all conditioned things are selfless.

body.text: svarūpāsiddhyāpi hetvabhāsanirūpaṇam
body.translated_text: Determination of Fallacious Reasons through Non-Establishment of Own-Nature

body.text: svarūpāsiddhayāpyasiddho hetvābhāso bhavati / yathā anityaśśabdaḥ cākṣuṣatvāditi / nanu vyāptyasiddhirapi dūṣaṇam, tenāpi pareṣṭārthāsiddheḥ / tatkiṃ nocyate? anaikāntikadūṣaṇenaiva gatārthatvāt pṛthaḍnoktam / tathā hi - na svalakṣaṇābhyāṃ vyāptirgrahītuṃ śakyā / svalakṣaṇasya deśakālākāraniyatatvenāpyanyatrānugamābhāvāt / api tu sādhyasādhanasāmānyābhyāmeva vyāptirgrahītavyā / tatra ca yadi sādhanaṃ sādhyena vyāptaṃ na pratīyate tadā sādhanaṃ ca syāt sādhyaṃ ca na syādityanaikāntikameva bhavati //
body.translated_text: A fallacious reason can also be one that is unestablished through non-establishment of own-nature. For example: 'Sound is impermanent because it is visible.' Now, non-establishment of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) is also a fault, since thereby the opponent's intended conclusion is not established. Why then is it not stated separately? Because it is subsumed under the three [types] — it is not stated separately.

body.text: apohanirūpaṇam, sāmānyanirasanaṃ ca
body.translated_text: Determination of <s>Apoha</s> (Exclusion), and Refutation of Universals

body.text: nanu sāmānyaṃ cedaprasiddhaṃ, tatkathaṃ sādhyasādhanasāmānyābhyāṃ sarvopasaṃhāravatī vyāptiḥ pramāṇena gṛhyate? naiṣa doṣaḥ / yato yādṛśaṃ sāmānyaṃ paraiḥ parikalpyate tādṛśaṃ pramāṇena bādhyata iti nābhyupeyate tatsaugataiḥ / na tu vyavahāraprasiddhamanyavyāvṛttilakṣaṇamapohasaṃjñitamapi / nanu ko 'yamapoho nāma? yathādhyavasāyaṃ bāhya eva ghaṭādirartha apoha ityabhidhīyate, apohyate 'smādanyadvijātīyamiti kṛtvā / yathāpratibhāsaṃ buddhyākāro vāpohaḥ, apohyate pṛthak kriyate 'smin buddhyākāre vijātīyamiti kṛtvā / yathātattvaṃ nivṛttimātraṃ prasajyarūpo vāpohaḥ, apohanamapoha iti kṛtvā /
body.translated_text: Objection: If universals (<s>sāmānya</s>) are not established, how can pervasion with complete enumeration, through the universals of the probandum and the probans, be grasped by valid means of knowledge? This is not a fault. Because the kind of universal that is conceptually constructed by the opponents is invalidated by valid means of knowledge — thus the Buddhists do not accept it. But [they do accept] what is well-known in conventional practice, characterized by the exclusion of others (<s>anyavyāvṛtti</s>), designated as <s>apoha</s>. Now, what is this <s>apoha</s>? In terms of determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>), the external object such as a pot is called <s>apoha</s>, because what is of a different class is excluded from it. In terms of appearance (<s>pratibhāsa</s>), the form in cognition is <s>apoha</s>, because what is of a different class is separated out, i.e., set apart, in that cognitive form. In terms of reality (<s>yathātattva</s>), mere exclusion — of the <s>prasajya</s> (implicative) type — is <s>apoha</s>, since the act of excluding is <s>apoha</s>.

body.text: nanu yathādhyavasāyaṃ vidhireva, tarhi kevalo visāya ityāgatam / na apohaviśiṣṭo vidhirabhipretaḥ / yattu gopratītau na gavātmā agavātmeti sāmarthyādapohaḥ paścānniścīyata iti vidhivādināṃ matam / anyāpohapratipattau ca sāmarthyādanyapoḍho gavādirartho 'vadhāryata iti nivṛttyapohavādināṃ matam / tanna yuktam, vyavahārakāle prathamaṃ vartamānasyāpi pratītikramādarśanāt / na hi vidhiṃ pratipadya kaścidarthāpattitaḥ paścādapohamavagacchati, apohaṃ vā pratipadya paścādanyāpoḍhamavagacchati / tasmāt gopratipattireva anyāpoḍha pratipattirucyate / yadyapi gośabdāduccaritādanyāpoḍhaśabdānullekha uktaḥ, tathāpi nāpratipattireva viśeṣaṇabhūtasyānyāpohasya / agavāpoḍha eva vastuni gośabdasya saṃketitatvāt / yathā nīlotpalasaṃketitendīvaraśabdāt utpalapratītau tatkāla eva nīlamasphuraṇamanivāryaṃ tathā gośabdādapyagavāpoḍha eva vastuni saṃketitāt gopratītau tulyakālameva viśeṣaṇatvāt apohasya agavāpoha- sphuraṇamanivāryam / yathā ca pratyakṣasya prasajyapratiṣedharūpābhāvagrahaṇamabhāva vikalpotpādanaśaktireva, tathā vidhivikalpānāmapi tadanurūpānuṣṭhānaśaktirevābhāvagrahaṇamabhidhīyate / anyathā yadi gośabdādarthapratipattikāle nāvagataḥ parāpohaḥ, kathaṃ tarhi anyaparihāreṇa pratipattā gavi vartatām / tatto gāṃ badhāneti codito 'śvānapi badhnīyāditi / tasmāt sthitametat,bāhyārtho 'dhyavasāyādeva śabdavācye vyavasthāpyate, na tu svalakṣaṇaparisphūrtyā, pratyakṣaddyeśakālākārāvasthāniyata pravyaktasvalakṣaṇāsphuraṇāt / yadāha nyāyaparameśvaraḥ - 'śabdenāvyāpṛtākṣasya buddhāvapratibhāsanāt /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If [<s>apoha</s>] in terms of determination is a positive entity alone, then [the word 'apoha'] has become merely a synonym [for a positive thing]. [Reply:] The intended [meaning] is not a positive entity qualified by <s>apoha</s>. Now, the view of the positivists is that in the cognition of a cow, the <s>apoha</s> — 'not the nature of a non-cow' — is subsequently ascertained through implication, but the nature of a cow [is cognized first]. And the view of the <s>anyāpoha</s>-proponents [of the negative <s>apoha</s> variety] is that through the cognition of 'exclusion of the other,' the object such as a cow, excluded from what is not a cow, is subsequently determined through implication. Both are unjustified, because there is no evidence of [such] a sequence in cognition at the time of practical usage. For no one, having cognized a positive entity, subsequently understands the <s>apoha</s> through implication; nor, having cognized the <s>apoha</s>, subsequently understands the thing excluded from others. Therefore, the cognition of a cow is itself the cognition of what is excluded from non-cows. Even though it is said that from the uttered word 'cow,' the word 'excluded from non-cow' does not explicitly appear, still the <s>apoha</s> which is a qualifier — namely, exclusion from non-cow — is not uncognized. Because the word 'cow' is conventionally assigned to a thing precisely as excluded from non-cows. Just as, from the word '<s>indīvara</s>' (blue lotus), which is conventionally assigned to a blue lotus, in the cognition of a lotus, blueness inevitably appears at that very moment; so too, from the word 'cow,' which is conventionally assigned to a thing precisely as excluded from non-cows, in the cognition of a cow, the flashing forth of the <s>apoha</s> of non-cow is inevitable at the same time, since <s>apoha</s> is a qualifier. And just as the grasping of absence — which has the form of a <s>prasajya</s> (simple) negation — by perception is its very power to generate a conceptual cognition of absence, so too for positive conceptual cognitions, the so-called grasping of absence is their very power to generate action corresponding to them. Otherwise, if the exclusion of others were not understood at the time of understanding the meaning from the word 'cow,' how would the person who understands act regarding the cow while excluding others? Then, when instructed to 'tie up the cow,' one would tie up horses too. Therefore, this stands: the external object is established in the word-referent through determination alone, not through the vivid appearance of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), because the clearly defined particular, restricted to the specific place, time, and form [present] in perception, does not flash forth [through words]. As the supreme lord of logic (<s>Dharmakīrti</s>) has said: 'Because, for one whose senses are not engaged, there is no appearance [of the particular] in cognition through words,

body.text: arthasya dṛṣṭāviva' iti //
body.translated_text: just as in the seeing of an object.'

body.text: kiñca svalakṣaṇātmani vastuni vācye sarvātmanā pratipatteḥ vidhiniṣedhayorayogaḥ / tasya hi sadbhāve astīti vyartham, nāstītyasamartham / asadbhāve tu nāstīti vyartham,astitya samartham / asti cāstyādipadaprayogaḥ / tasmāt paramārthato na svalakṣaṇaṃ śabdairabhidhīyata iti sthitam //
body.translated_text: Moreover, if the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) were the referent of words in its entirety, affirmation and negation would be impossible. For if it exists, 'it exists' is futile; 'it does not exist' is incapable. And if it does not exist, 'it does not exist' is futile; 'it exists' is incapable. Yet there is indeed the use of words such as 'exists' and the like. Therefore, it is established that in ultimate reality, the particular is not expressed by words.

body.text: nanu yathā pratyakṣeṇa ghaṭasvarūpe gṛhīte 'paścāttatraiva kṣaṇikatvādiniścayārtha pramāṇāntaraṃ pravartate, tathā vṛkṣaśabdena vṛkṣatvāṃśe pratipādite satvāṃśaniścayārthameva sadādipadaprayogo bhaviṣyatīti cet, na / pratyakṣasyāniśyātmakatvādanabhyastasvarūpaviṣaye pramāṇāntaraṃ vartata iti yuktam / vikalpasya tu svayaṃ niśyātmakatvāt, gṛhīte svarūpe kiṃ pramāṇāntareṇa paraṃ grahītavyamiti //
body.translated_text: Objection: Just as, after the own-nature of a pot is grasped by perception, another means of knowledge operates upon that very [pot] for the purpose of ascertaining momentariness and the like, so too, after the tree-aspect has been conveyed by the word 'tree,' the use of words such as 'exists' will serve to ascertain the existence-aspect — [is this not the case]? No. Because perception is not of a determinate nature, it is reasonable that another means of knowledge operates upon an object whose own-nature has not been fully comprehended. But since conceptual cognition is itself of a determinate nature, once its own-nature has been grasped, what further is there to grasp by another means of knowledge?

body.text: paraparikalpitasāmānyanirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of Universals as Conceived by the Opponents

body.text: yādṛśaṃ sāmānyaṃ paraiḥ parikalpyate, anekavyaktisamavetaṃ dṛśyamekaṃ nityaṃ tādṛśasya sattāsādhakaṃ na kiñcitpramāṇāmupalabhāmahe / tataḥ saditi vyavasthāpayituṃ tanna yuktam / tathā hi - gavādivyaktyanubhavakāle varṇāsaṃsthānādyātmakaṃ vyaktisvarūpamapahāya nānyat kiñcidekamanuyāyi pratyakṣe bhāsate / tādṛśasyānubhavābhāvāt / nāpi svalakṣaṇānubhānantaramekākāraparāmarśapratyayāt anyathānupapattyā sāmānyaparikalpanaṃ yuktisaṅgatam / vyaktibhya eva svahetudattaśaktibhyo 'sya pratyayasya paramparayotpatteḥ / bhede 'pi kāścideva vyaktayo 'sya jananāya samarthāḥ, na sarvāḥ, ityatra kāryakāraṇabhāvasya pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ dṛṣṭasyātivartayitumaśakyatvāt / dṛṣṭaṃ cedaṃ sāmarthyaṃ bhedāviśeṣe 'pi kāsāñcideva vyaktīnām / yathā jvarādipraśamane guḍūcīnimbādīnām / yathoktam - 'ekapratyavamarśārthajñānādyekārthasādhane /
body.translated_text: We do not find any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) that establishes the existence of the kind of <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) conceived by the opponents — one that is inherent in many particulars, perceptible, single, and eternal. Therefore it is not reasonable to establish that it exists. For when experiencing particulars such as cows, nothing other than the particular's own form — consisting of color, shape, and so forth — appears in perception as a single accompanying entity, since there is no experience of such a thing. Nor is it logically consistent to postulate a universal on the basis of a unitary conceptual cognition arising after the experience of <s>svalakṣaṇas</s> (unique particulars), through the impossibility of accounting for it otherwise, because this cognition arises through a causal chain from the particulars themselves, which possess capacities bestowed by their own causes. Even though they are different, only certain particulars are capable of generating this cognition, not all — and here the causal relation cannot be overridden, since it is established through perception and non-apprehension. This capacity is observed to belong to only certain particulars despite the absence of a difference [in universal], just as <s>guḍūcī</s>, <s>nimba</s>, and so forth [are effective] in alleviating fever and the like. As it is said:

body.text: bhede 'pi niyatāḥ kecitsvabhāvenendriyādivat' // iti //
body.translated_text: "Even in difference, some are determined by their own nature, like sense faculties and so forth." Thus.

body.text: kiñca sarvagate vijātīyād vyāvṛtte satyapi sāmānye kiṃ bhedāviśeṣe 'pi govyaktiṣveva samavetaṃ tat sāmānyaṃ tatraiva caikākārāṃ buddhiṃ janayatīti praśne svabhāvenaivetyuttaraṃ parasya / tacca pramāṇāsaṅgatam / asmākaṃ tu svabhāvenottaraṃ pramāṇāsiddhatvāt yuktisaṅgatameva //
body.translated_text: Moreover, even if a universal exists that pervades everything and is excluded from what is heterogeneous, when the question is asked — why does that universal, though there is no difference [among instances], inhere only in cow-particulars and generate a uniform cognition only there? — the opponent's answer is "by its very nature." But that is unsupported by <s>pramāṇa</s>. Our answer "by its own nature," however, is logically consistent precisely because [we do not posit] anything unestablished by <s>pramāṇa</s>.

body.text: tathedamaparaṃ jātisādhanāya sādhanaṃ parasya / yad viśiṣṭaṃ jñānaṃ tad viśeṣaṇagrahaṇanāntarīyakam, yathā daṇḍijñānam / viśiṣṭajñānaṃ cedaṃ gaurayamityarthataḥ kāryahetuḥ / atrocyate -
body.translated_text: Likewise, here is another proof by the opponent for establishing <s>jāti</s> (universal class): whatever is a qualified cognition necessarily involves the apprehension of a qualifier, like the cognition of a staff-bearer. And this cognition 'this is a cow' is a qualified cognition — thus, in substance, this is a <s>kāryahetu</s> (effect-based reason). To this we reply:

body.text: viśiṣṭabuddherbhinnaviśeṣaṇagrahaṇanāntarīyakatvaṃ sādhyaṃ, viśeṣaṇamātrānubhavanāntarīyakatvaṃ vā / prathamapakṣe pratyakṣabādhā / vastugrāhiṇi pratyakṣe ubhayapratibhāsābhāvāt / viśiṣṭabuddhitvaṃ ca sāmānyamityanaikāntiko hetuḥ syāt,bhinnaviśeṣaṇagrahaṇamantareṇāpi tasya darśanāt / yathā svarūpavānayaṃ ghaṭaḥ, gotvasāmānyamiti vā / dvitīyapakṣe tu siddhasādhanam, svarūpavān ghaṭa ityādivat gotvādijātimān piṇḍa iti parikalpitabhedamupādāya viśeṣaṇaviśeṣya bhāvasyeṣṭatvāt /
body.translated_text: Is the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) that qualified cognition necessarily involves apprehension of a separate qualifier, or merely that it involves apprehension of any qualifier whatsoever? In the first case, there is contradiction by perception, since in perception, which grasps real things, the appearance of both [qualifier and qualified as separate entities] is absent. And the reason would be <s>anaikāntika</s> (inconclusive), since qualified cognition can be observed even without the apprehension of a separate qualifier — as in 'this pot has its own form' or 'this has the universal cowness.' In the second case, it would be <s>siddhasādhana</s> (proving what is already established),

body.text: agovyāvṛttyanubhavabhāvitvāt gaurayamiti vyavahārasya / tadevaṃ ato 'pi sādhanānna sāmānyasiddhiriti / tadevaṃ paraparikalpitasāmānyasya vicārāsahatvāt, atadrūpaparāvṛttavastumātrameva sāmānyamapohaśabdavācyaṃ vyavahārāṅgaṃ yathādhyavasāyamanavadyamiti sthitam /
body.translated_text: since the usage 'this is a cow' arises from the experience of exclusion from non-cow. Thus, even from this proof, the universal is not established. Therefore, since the universal as conceived by the opponents cannot withstand critical examination, it is established that mere things defined by exclusion from what is not their form — the real <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), expressible by the word <s>apoha</s> (exclusion) — serve as the basis for conventional usage and are, as determined, unobjectionable.

body.text: sāmānyasya niṣedhāya prayogaḥ punarevaṃ kartavyaḥ - yadyatropalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaṃ sannopalabhyate tattatra asadvyavahāraviṣayaḥ,yathā turaṅgamottamāṃge śṛṅgaṃ, nopalabhyate copalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaṃ sāmānyaṃ paridṛśyamānāsu vyaktiṣviti svabhāvānupalabdhiḥ / na cāsiddhasambhāvanā / varṇasaṃsthānalakṣaṇaṃ vyaktisvarūpamapahāya dvitīyasyānuyāyino rūpasya nipuṇamapi nirūpyamāṇasya sarvathā darśanābhāvāt, nāpi jñānavaddarśanābhāve 'pi pratyakṣasiddhatvamasyābhidhātumucitam / jñānaṃ hi svasaṃvedanapramāṇasiddham, na tu cakṣurvijñānagrāhyam / idaṃ [tu sāmānyaṃ] cakṣurvijñānagrāhyamarthadharmatvāt / pratyakṣaṃ ca parairiṣṭamiti / tadevaṃ paraparikalpitasāmānyasya vicārāsahatvāt, atadrūpaparāvṛttavastumātrameva sāmānyamuktam / tasmāt sarvaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ vastu paraparikalpitasāmānyena śūnyamiti sthitam //
body.translated_text: For the negation of universals, the formal proof should be constructed thus: whatever satisfies the conditions for perceptibility yet is not perceived at a given place is the object of the designation 'non-existent' there — like a horn on the head of a fine horse. And the universal, though satisfying the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived in the visible particulars — this is <s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of an entity's own nature). Nor is there the possibility of the reason being unestablished, because when one carefully examines, setting aside the particular's own form characterized by color and shape, there is absolutely no perception of a second accompanying form,

body.text: īśvarasādhananirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of the proof for <s>Īśvara</s> (God)

body.text:
nāpi kenacidbuddhimatoparacittamityapi vijñeyam /
tathā hi - asya jagataḥ karttā bhavan nityo vā bhavedanityo vā / tatra na tāvannityo yuktaḥ, nitye karttari samarthe sati sargasthitipralayānāṃ niyamena yaugapadyaprasaṅgāt / yena hi svarūpeṇa sthitipralayayoḥ sa karttā tadasya svarūpaṃ sargakāle 'pi sannihitamiti tadaiva sthitipralayau kuryāt / sahakārivirahānna karotīti cet, tadasat / na hi nityena sahakāriṇā kadācidapyayaṃ virahitaḥ sadā sannihitatvāt / nāpyanityena sahakāriṇā virahitaḥ, anityasahakāriṇo 'pi tadāyattajanmatvāt / tata ekadā sarvakaraṇādiprasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: nor should it be supposed by anyone intelligent that another mind [i.e., God] exists. For the maker of this world would be either eternal or non-eternal. In the first place, an eternal [maker] is not reasonable, because if the maker is eternal and capable, there would be the absurd consequence that creation, preservation, and destruction would necessarily occur simultaneously. For the very nature by which he is the maker of preservation and destruction — that nature is also present at the time of creation, so he should perform preservation and destruction at that very time. If [objected that] he does not act due to the absence of auxiliary causes — that is wrong. For in the case of an eternal [being],

body.text: nanu buddhimattvādīśvarasya naiṣa doṣaḥ / buddhiśūnyo hi svasattāmātrajanyaṃ kāryamakrameṇaiva kuryāt / buddhimāṃstu karttumīśāno 'pi anicchanna karotīti kastasyopālambhaḥ? ucyate - tā apīcchāḥ svasattāmātranibandhanāḥ kiṃ na karotīti sa evāsyopālambhaḥ / atha svarūpeṇa sāmarthye satyapi eṣa eva tasya svabhāvaḥ, yatsahakārilakṣaṇayāgantukaśaktyā vinā na karotīti cet, tarhi mātāpi sati vandhyā sā prakṛtyaivaitadapi vaktavyaṃ bhavedbhavatāmiti yatkiñcidetat //
body.translated_text: "But," [the opponent says,] "since <s>Īśvara</s> is intelligent, this fault does not apply. For one devoid of intelligence would produce effects born solely from his own existence without sequence. But one who is capable of acting yet does not wish to act does not act — what blame is there for him?" We reply: those desires too are dependent solely on his own existence — why does he not [always] act? That is precisely the objection against him. And if [you say that] although having the capacity by his own nature, this is simply his nature — that without adventitious power in the form of auxiliary causes he does not act — then even a mother being [i.e., capable of bearing], she would be barren,

body.text: nanveṣa eva kāryasvabhāvaḥ, kevalāt samarthādapi nodeti, sahakāriṇamapekṣyaiva paścādbhavati [nāsyopālambha iti] tanna yuktam / samartho hi sahakāryapekṣāmanādṛtya balādeva kāryaṃ kuryāt / anyathā [hyasya] asamarthatvaprasaṅgāt / nityasya kramakāritvaniṣedhanam nāpi nityaḥ krameṇa kāryakārīti yuktam, nirapekṣatvāt / yadāha diṅmaṇḍalavikhyātakīrtirdharmakīrtiḥ -
body.translated_text: "But," [the opponent says,] "this is the very nature of effects — they do not arise even from one who is capable alone, but arise only afterward, depending on auxiliary causes. [So there is no blame.]" This is not reasonable. For one who is capable should produce the effect by force, disregarding the need for auxiliaries. Otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of his being incapable. Refutation of gradual production by a permanent entity: nor is it reasonable that a permanent entity produces effects gradually, because it is independent [of conditions]. As the illustrious <s>Dharmakīrti</s>, whose fame pervades the quarters, has said:

children.translated_text: "For a permanent entity, since it is independent, gradual production is not possible;
at times of action and inaction, its nature being identical." Thus.

body.text: etena ātmādīnāmakṣaṇikānāṃ ghaṭādīnāṃ kṣaṇikānāṃ ca krameṇa kāryakaraṇaṃ pratyuktam / na cātra pratyakṣavirodhaḥ, pratyakṣeṇākṣaṇikasya grahaṇāyogāt / na hi kṣaṇikaṃ pratyakṣamakṣaṇikamīkṣituṃ kṣamate / anikakṣaṇavyāpāro hyakṣaṇikaḥ / sa kathamekakṣaṇabhāvinādhyakṣeṇa grahītuṃ śakyaḥ / na hi prāgūrdhvaṃ cāvasthānamadhunā prakāśate / tasyāpyadhunātanatāprasaṅgāt / janmavināśāvadhipratibhāsaprasaṅgāditi nedaṃ pratyakṣaṃ pūrvāparakālavyāptamarthaṃ kañcidapi grahītumalam /
body.translated_text: By this, gradual production of effects by non-momentary entities such as the <s>ātman</s> (self) and by momentary entities such as pots and the like is also refuted. Nor is there any contradiction with perception here, since a non-momentary entity cannot be grasped by perception. For momentary perception is not capable of perceiving a non-momentary entity. A non-momentary entity, indeed, has its activity spanning more than one moment. How then can it be grasped by direct perception, which exists only for a single moment? For the previous and subsequent states do not shine forth in the present, since there would be the absurd consequence of those too being present.

body.text: pratyabhijñānasya pratyakṣatvaṃ nirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of <s>pratyabhijñāna</s> (recognition) as being perception

body.text: etena pratyabhijñānasyāpratyakṣatvamākhyātam / sākṣātkāri hi jñānaṃ pratyakṣam / na ca prāgavasthamadhunā sākṣātkartavyam, api tu smartavyam / na ca smaraṇasvarūpam pratyakṣam / atha mataṃ bhavedidaṃ smaraṇaṃ yadidānīntanamavasthānaṃ na sākṣātkuryāt, tatsākṣātkaraṇapravaṇaṃ kathamidaṃ smaraṇaṃ nāma? yadāha bhaṭṭaḥ -
body.translated_text: By this, it is also declared that <s>pratyabhijñāna</s> (recognition) is not perception. For perception is cognition that directly apprehends. And what existed previously should not be directly apprehended now, but rather should be remembered. And memory in its essential nature is not perception. Now, if this memory did not directly apprehend the present state, then being inclined toward direct apprehension of that [present state], how could this be called memory? As <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> [Dharmakīrti] has said:

children.translated_text: "Regarding what was merely previously known, memory arises [thinking] 'that';
but 'that very same one' — this [recognition] differs from [mere memory]." Thus.

body.text:
smaraṇagrahaṇasvarūpaṃ tarhi pratyabhijñānaṃ syāt, na tu grahaṇasvarūpameva / smaryamāṇe grahaṇāyogāt, gṛhyamāṇe ca smaraṇāyogāt / na caikasya smaraṇagrahaṇe sambhavataḥ, parasparavirodhāt / yena hi svarūpeṇa smaraṇaṃ na tena svarūpeṇa grahaṇamityanunmattena śakyate vaktum / rūpāntareṇa caikasya smaraṇagrahaṇe na syātām / bhāve 'pi pratyakṣāpratyakṣe syātām / na tu smaryamāṇe pratyakṣameva, pratyakṣāyogāt / tasmāt pratyabhijñāpratyayo bhrānta eva, nirviṣayatvāt /
prayogaścaivam - yaḥ pratyabhijñāpratyayaḥ sa tattvato naikālambanaḥ, yathā lūnapunarjātatṛṇādiṣu / pratyabhijñā pratyayaścāyaṃ tadevedaṃ nīlādīti pratyaya iti viruddhavyāptopalabdhiḥ / ekatvānekatvayoḥ parasparavirodhāt tadviṣayakasaṃvedanayorapi virodhaḥ tenaikālambanatvena anekālambanatvaviruddhena anekālambanatvena pūrvoktyā nītyā pratyabhijñāpratyayo vyāpta iti na pratyabhijñānaṃ kṣaṇikānumānabādhakam / na ca keśādiṣvapi sāmānyālambanatayā ekālambanatvam keśādivyaktereva pratyabhijñāyamānatvāt / sāmānye pratyabhijñāyamāne tadevedaṃ keśādīti syāt, na tadevedaṃ keśādīti / ata evaikālambanatve pratyabhijñāpratyayasya krametarābhyāmutpattivirodhāt, viruddhānaikāntikatve nāśaṅkanīye / na ca pratyabhijñānameva tadavasthāpakam, yasyaiva vicāryamāṇatvāt / tasmāt sthitametat nityaḥ kartā nāstīti / yadi nityaḥ kartā jagato na kāraṇaṃ, kimasya tarhi kāraṇam?
body.translated_text:
Then pratyabhijñāna (recognition) would have the nature of both remembering and apprehending, not merely the nature of apprehension alone — because apprehension is impossible with respect to what is being remembered, and remembering is impossible with respect to what is being apprehended. And both remembering and apprehending cannot occur in a single entity, due to their mutual contradiction. For one who is not insane can state that the nature by which there is remembering is not the nature by which there is apprehension. And if remembering and apprehending occurred in a single entity through a different nature, they would be both perceptual and non-perceptual even if they existed. But what is being remembered is certainly not perceptual, since perception is impossible in that case. Therefore, the cognition of recognition is indeed erroneous, because it lacks a real object.
The formal argument is as follows: any cognition of recognition does not in reality have a single object, just as in the case of grass that has been cut and grown again, and so forth. And this cognition of recognition — the cognition 'this very thing is that blue, etc.' — involves the apprehension of a property pervaded by a contradictory property. Since oneness and multiplicity are mutually contradictory, the cognitions having them as objects are also contradictory; therefore the cognition of recognition is pervaded by having multiple objects through the contradiction with having a single object, and by having multiple objects through the method stated previously. Thus recognition does not obstruct the inference of momentariness. Nor is there a single object on the basis of a <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) even in the case of hair and the like, since it is the particular instance of hair, etc. that is recognized. If a <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) were recognized, it would be 'this very thing is that hair, etc.' — not 'this very thing is this particular hair, etc.' For this very reason, since the cognition of recognition having a single object contradicts arising either sequentially or otherwise, one should not suspect the fallacy of being contradictory or inconclusive. Nor does recognition itself establish that [permanence], since it is precisely recognition that is under examination. Therefore it is established that there is no eternal agent. If an eternal agent is not the cause of the world, then what is its cause?

body.text: sattvānāṃ śubhakarmaṇaḥ jagataḥ kāraṇatvasamarthanam
body.translated_text: Establishing that the <s>karma</s> (action) of beings, consisting of meritorious deeds, is the cause of the world

body.text: sattvānāṃ śubhāśubhākhyaṃ karma / yathoktam -
body.translated_text: The <s>karma</s> (action) of beings is called meritorious and demeritorious. As it is said:

children.translated_text: The mind alone constructs the world of beings and the vessel world, in a most wondrous manner.

children.text: karmajaṃ hi jagaduktamaśeṣaṃ karma cittamavadhūya na cāsti // iti //
children.translated_text: For the entire world is said to be born of <s>karma</s> (action), and <s>karma</s> does not exist apart from mind.

body.text: vaibhāṣikamāśritya punarbhagavatā sarvajñena coktam -
body.translated_text: Furthermore, relying on the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> view, the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One), the omniscient one, has also said:

children.translated_text: Space, the two cessations — these three are eternal and <s>asaṃskṛta</s> (unconditioned).
All that is <s>saṃskṛta</s> (conditioned) is momentary, devoid of self, and without an agent.

body.text: sarvajñasamarthanam bhavaparamparāsamarthanaṃ ca
body.translated_text: Establishing the omniscient one, and establishing the succession of existences

body.text: nanu sarvajñasiddhau hi tadvacanaṃ nidarśanīkartumucitam / sarvajñasiddhaye kiṃ pramāṇamiti cet? ucyate / yo yaḥ sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsakalitacetoguṇaḥ sa sarvaḥ sphuṭībhāvayogyaḥ, yathā yuvatyākāraḥ kāminaḥ puruṣasya / yathoktābhyāsakalitacetoguṇāścāmī caturāryasatyaviṣayākārā iti svabhāvahetuḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, if the omniscience [of the <s>Buddha</s>] is established, then it is appropriate to cite his words as authority. If asked: what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for establishing omniscience? The reply is: whoever has a mental quality cultivated through practice that is devoted, uninterrupted, and prolonged — all such [qualities] are capable of becoming manifest, just as the image of a young woman [becomes vivid] for a man filled with desire. And these mental qualities having the form of the four noble truths are cultivated through the aforesaid practice — this is a <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (essential-nature reason).

body.text: na tāvadāśrayadvāreṇa hetudvāreṇa vāsiddhasambhāvanā / saṅkalparuḍhānāṃ caturāryasatyaviṣayākārāṇāṃ dharmiṇāṃ cetoguṇamātrasya ca hetoḥ pratyātmavedyatvāt / na caiṣa viruddhaḥ, sapakṣe kāminyākāre sambhavāt / na cānaikāntikaḥ, abhyāsena sahitacetoguṇasphuṭapratibhāsayoḥ kāraṇakāryayoḥ kumbhakāraghaṭayoriva sarvopasaṃhāreṇa pratyakṣānupalambhataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhau abhyāsasahitacetoguṇatvasya sādhanasya sphuṭapratibhāsakāraṇayogyatayā vyāptisiddheḥ / tathā hi - vyāptyadhikaraṇe kāmāturavartini yuvatyākāre sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsasahitacetoguṇāt pūrvamanupalabdhiḥ sphuṭābhatvasya paścādabhyāsasaṃvedanaṃ,sphuṭābhasaṃvedanamiti trividhapratyakṣānupalambhasādhyaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ sphuṭapratibhāsābhyāsa sahitacittākārayorityupapannā sarvopasaṃhāravatī vyāptiḥ / ato 'naikāntikatvābhāvāt anavadyo hetuḥ //
body.translated_text: There is no unestablished possibility either through the basis or through the reason. Because the four noble truth-aspects as <s>dharmin</s> (subject), which are established through resolve, and the reason which is merely a mental quality, are each known through personal experience. Nor is this [reason] contradictory, since it occurs in the positive example of the image of a beloved woman. Nor is it inconclusive, because the causal relation between the mental quality combined with practice and clear manifestation is established through universal induction by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anupalambha</s> (non-apprehension) — just like the relation between a potter and a pot. For in the locus of pervasion, namely in the image of a young woman for one tormented by desire: first there is non-apprehension of clear manifestation before the mental quality combined with devoted, uninterrupted, and prolonged practice; then there is awareness of practice; then there is awareness of clear manifestation — thus the causal relation between clear manifestation and the mental form combined with practice is established by threefold perception-and-non-apprehension, and the pervasion with universal induction is established. Therefore, due to the absence of inconclusiveness, the reason is faultless.

body.text:
nanvanena sādhanena caturāryasatyākārāṇāṃ sākṣātkaraṇāt caturāryasatyākārasākṣatkārī vivakṣitassarvajñaḥ sidhyati, na tvaviśeṣeṇa sarvadharmasākṣatkārī, tatastatsiddhaye sādhanāntaramabhidheyam /
ucyate - yatpramāṇasaṃvādi niścitārthaṃ vacanaṃ, tat sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa vā tadarthasākṣatkārijñānapūrvakaṃ, yathā dahano dāhaka iti vacanam, pramāṇasaṃvādi niścitārtha cedaṃ vacanaṃ, kṣaṇikāḥ sarvasaṃskārā iti arthataḥ kāryahetuḥ / nāsyāsiddhiḥ, sarvadharmakṣaṇabhaṅgaprasādhanādasya vacanasya satyārthatvāt / nāpi viruddhaḥ, sapekṣe bhāvāt / na cānaikāntikatā, vacanamātrasya saṃśayaviparyāsapūrvakatve 'pi pramāṇa saṃvādi] niścitārthasya [vacanasya] sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa vā tadarthasākṣātkārijñānapūrvakatvena pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāmupalambhāt / anyathā dhūmādāvapi hetutyāgaprasaṅgādaśeṣakāryahetūcchedaprasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text:
Objection: by this proof, since only the direct realization of the four noble truth-aspects is established, the omniscient one intended is one who directly realizes the four noble truth-aspects — but not one who directly realizes all <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) without distinction. Therefore another proof should be stated for establishing that.
Reply: a statement that accords with <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) and has a determined meaning is preceded — directly or indirectly — by knowledge that directly realizes its referent, just as the statement 'fire burns.' If this statement accords with <s>pramāṇa</s> and has a determined meaning, then 'all <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned things) are momentary' — this is essentially a <s>kāryahetu</s> (effect-reason). There is no unestablishedness of this, because the statement has a true meaning due to the proof of the momentary destruction of all <s>dharmas</s>. Nor is it contradictory, since it exists in the positive example. Nor is there inconclusiveness, because although mere statements may be preceded by doubt or error, a statement that accords with <s>pramāṇa</s> and has a determined meaning is apprehended through perception and non-apprehension as being preceded — directly or indirectly — by knowledge that directly realizes its referent. Otherwise, the consequence of abandoning the reason even in cases like smoke would lead to the consequence of the destruction of all effect-reason relations.

body.text: bhavaparamparānirūpaṇam
body.translated_text: Examination of the succession of existences

body.text: syādetat / anekabhavaparamparālakṣaṇena dīrghakālena bhāvyasya saṅkalpāruḍhasya sphuṭābhatvaṃ sambhāvyate / bhavaparamparāsiddhaye tu kiṃ pramāṇam? ucyate / yaccittaṃ tat cittāntaraṃ pratisandhatte, yathedānīntanaṃ cittam / cittaṃ ca maraṇakālabhāvīti svabhāvahetuḥ / na cārhaccaramacittena vyabhicāraḥ / tasyāgamamātrapratītatvāt niḥ kleśacittāntarajananādvā / hetoḥ kleśe sati / viśeṣāpekṣaṇādi tyanāgatabhavasiddhiḥ / iha pūrvajanmābhyāsāt tapodānādhyayanādau sarvasattvānāmabhyāse pravṛttiriti pravādaḥ / tatastatsiddhaye pramāṇamucyate - yaccittaṃ tat cittāntarapūrvakaṃ yathedānīntanaṃ cittam / cittaṃ ca janmasamayabhāvītyarthataḥ kāryahetuḥ //vaibhāṣikamatanirūpaṇam
body.translated_text: One might say: it is conceivable that what is to be cultivated, established through resolve, becomes clearly manifest over a long duration characterized by a succession of many existences. But what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for establishing the succession of existences? The reply is: whatever is mind connects with another mind [in the next life], just as the present mind does. And the mind exists at the time of death — this is a <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (essential-nature reason). Nor is there deviation through the final mind of an <s>Arhat</s>, since that is known only through scripture, or because it generates another mind free from afflictions when the cause — namely affliction — is present. Due to requiring a specific condition and so forth, future existence is established. In this world, due to practice in previous births, all beings engage in the practice of austerity, charity, study, and the like — this is the teaching. Therefore, the <s>pramāṇa</s> for establishing that is stated: whatever is mind is preceded by another mind, just as the present mind. And the mind exists at the time of birth — this is essentially a <s>kāryahetu</s> (effect-reason). Examination of the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> view:

body.text: nanu tattvasākṣātkāraṇānmuktiḥ / tattvaṃ caikameva, yathoktam -
body.translated_text: Now, liberation comes from the direct realization of reality. And reality is one alone, as it is said:

body.text: `muktistu śūnyatādṛṣṭistadarthāśeṣabhāvanā' iti /
body.translated_text: Liberation is the seeing of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) and the complete cultivation of its meaning.

body.text: tatkathaṃ sarvajñadvaitaṃ, bauddhaprabhedaśceti? naiṣa doṣaḥ / yasmātsarvametad bhūtārthe sattvānavatārayituṃ bhagavatā pratipāditam / tathā hi vaibhāṣikāṇāṃ matam -
body.translated_text: Then how is there a duality of omniscient ones, and divisions among Buddhists? This is not a fault. Because all of this was taught by the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) in order to lead beings to the true meaning. Thus, the view of the <s>Vaibhāṣikas</s> is:

children.translated_text: Space, the two cessations — these three are eternal and <s>asaṃskṛta</s> (unconditioned).
All that is <s>saṃskṛta</s> (conditioned) is momentary, devoid of self, and without an agent.

body.text: sautrāntikānāṃ matam
body.translated_text: The view of the <s>Sautrāntikas</s>

body.text:
jñānamevedaṃ sarvaṃ nīlādyākāreṇa pratibhāsate, na bāhyo 'rthaḥ, jaḍasya prakāśāyogāt /
yathoktam -
body.translated_text:
All this is nothing but cognition, which appears with the form of blue and the like — there is no external object, since what is inert cannot illuminate.
As it is said:

body.text: `svakārajñānajanakā dṛśyā nendriyagocārāḥ' // iti //
body.translated_text: The visible things that generate cognition bearing their own form are not within the range of the senses.

body.text: alaṅkāreṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: <s>Alaṅkāra</s> [i.e., <s>Dharmakīrti</s> in the <s>Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra</s>] has also said:

children.text: yadi saṃvedyate nīlaṃ kathaṃ bāhyaṃ taducyate /
children.translated_text: If blue is cognized, how can it be called external?

children.text: na cetsaṃvedyate nīlaṃ kathaṃ bāhyaṃ taducyate //
children.translated_text: And if blue is not cognized, how can it be called external?

body.text: nanu yadi prakāśamānaṃ jñānamevadaṃ, tadāsti bāhyo 'rtha iti kutaḥ? bāhyārthasiddhistu syādvayatirekataḥ / na hi sarvatra sarvadā nīlādaya ākārāḥ prakāśante /
body.translated_text: Objection: if what appears is nothing but cognition itself, then on what grounds is there an external object? The establishment of an external object would be through the method of difference. For the forms of blue and the like do not appear everywhere and at all times.

body.text: na caitat svopādānamātrabalabhāvitve sati yujyate / niyataviṣaye pravṛttyayogāt / tasmādasti kiñcideṣāṃ samanantarapratyayavyatiriktaṃ yadbalena kvacit kadācit bhavantīti śakyamavasātum / sa eva bāhyo 'rtha iti, na punarasau bāhyo 'rthaḥ avayavī, guṇādayo dharmāḥ dravyāśrayiṇaḥ parābhimatāḥ, navavidhaṃ dravyaṃ paramāṇāvo veti / tatra na tāvat guṇādayaḥ, dravyaniṣedhenaiva teṣāṃ niṣedhāt / na cāsati samavāyini dravye samavāya iti tadduṣaṇamatra nādriyate / dravyaṃ ca pṛthivyāpastejovāyurākāśaṃ kālo digātmā mana iti navavidham /
body.translated_text: But this is not tenable if [cognition] arises solely by the power of its own material cause alone, since engagement with a determinate object would be impossible. Therefore, it can be concluded that there is something other than the <s>samanantarapratyaya</s> (immediately preceding condition) of these [cognitions], by the power of which they arise in certain places and at certain times. That is the external object. However, that external object is not a whole possessing parts (<s>avayavī</s>), nor qualities and other properties inhering in substance as maintained by others, nor substance of nine kinds, nor atoms. Among these, first, qualities and the rest [are refuted], since their negation follows from the negation of substance alone. And since there is no <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) in the absence of an inherent substance, that refutation is not elaborated here. And substance is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, self, and mind.

body.text: ātmākāśakāladiṅmanasāṃ nirasanam
body.translated_text: Refutation of self, space, time, direction, and mind

body.text: tatrātmaniṣedhāyedamapi sādhanam - yatkādācitkaṃ jñānaṃ tatkādācitkakāraṇapūrvakam, yathā saudāminījñānam / kādācitkaṃ cedamahaṃkārajñānamityarthataḥ kāryahetuḥ / nāyamasiddhaḥ ahaṃkāre dharmiṇi jñānatvasya pratyakṣasiddhatvāt / nāpi kādācitkaviśeṣaṇamasiddham, sarvadāhamiti jñānābhāvāt / nāpi viruddhaḥ, sapakṣe darśanāt / na cānaikāntikaḥ, dhūmapāvakayoriva kādācitkajñānakādācitkakāraṇayoḥ pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ vyāptisiddheḥ / kādācitkajñānasya cākādācitkakāraṇādutpattau kādācitkakāraṇādanutpattiprasaṅgaḥ / aniyatahetukatāyāṃ cāhetukatāprasaṅgaḥ, tathāpyanaikāntikatve prasiddhadhūmādiheturapyanaikāntikaḥ syāt, viśeṣābhāvāt / api cāhaṃkārasya akādācitkakāraṇapūrvakatve sadaivodayaprasaṅgaḥ / kāraṇasya kurvadrūpatvāt, akurvataścopacārataḥ kāraṇatvāt, kurvadakurvatoraikyābhāvāt / bhāve vā kurvato 'pyakurvadrūpatāpattiḥ, tatsvabhāvatvāt / kiñcāhaṃkārasya akādācitka kāraṇādutpāde yugapadevotpādaprasaṅgaḥ, avyagrasāmagrīkatvāt / nanvahaṃkārasyālambanamātmā na kāraṇamiti cenna / akāraṇasyālambanatvāyogādatiprasaṅgāditi //
body.translated_text: Now, for the refutation of the <s>ātman</s> (self), this proof is also [offered]: Whatever cognition is occasional must be preceded by an occasional cause, like the cognition of lightning. And this cognition of ego-sense (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>) is occasional — thus, in substance, [this is] an inference from effect to cause. This [reason] is not unestablished, since the property of being a cognition (<s>jñānatva</s>) is established by direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) with respect to the subject, ego-sense. Nor is the qualifier 'occasional' unestablished, since there is no cognition 'I am' at all times. Nor is [the reason] contradictory, since it is observed in the similar instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>). Nor is it inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), since the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) between occasional cognition and occasional cause is established through perception and non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>), just as between smoke and fire. Moreover, if occasional cognition were to arise from a non-occasional cause, then the absurd consequence would follow that it would not arise from an occasional cause either. And if the causal relation were indeterminate, the absurd consequence of causelessness would follow; and even so, if [this reasoning led to] inconclusiveness, then even well-established reasons like smoke would be inconclusive, since there is no distinguishing feature. Furthermore, if ego-sense were preceded by a non-occasional cause, the absurd consequence would be that it arises at all times, because a cause has the nature of producing [its effect]; and what does not produce is a cause only figuratively (<s>upacāra</s>); and there is no identity between what produces and what does not produce. Or, even if [the cause] exists, [there would be] the absurd consequence that even what produces takes on the nature of not producing, since that is its essential nature. Moreover, if ego-sense arose from a non-occasional cause, the absurd consequence would be simultaneous arising of all [ego-cognitions], since the causal conditions would be complete without delay. If one objects that the <s>ātman</s> is merely the object (<s>ālambana</s>) of ego-sense and not its cause — no, that is not so, because what is not a cause cannot logically be an object, and because of overextension.

body.text: atha kimākāśaṃ nāma kiñcidvastubhūtamasti? uta nāsti vā? nāstyevaitat / yatra hi sapratighaṃ dravyamasti na tatrākāśamavakāśaṃ vā dadāti / yatra nāsti tatra tadabhāvādevāvakāśaḥ siddha iti kva vākāśamavakāśaṃ dadyāt? [yasmādavakāśapradamākāśaṃ bhaṇyate] tasmāt satyasmin sarvadā sarvathā sarvatrāvakāśaḥ syāt / na caitadasti / tasmānnāstyevākāśamiti pratīmaḥ / etacca vaibhāṣīkamatapekṣya dūṣaṇamuktam / paraistvākāśaṃ śabdaguṇakamiṣyate / taccaikamiti cet samānadeśatvāt sarvaśabdānāṃ vibhāgena śravaṇaṃ na syāt / tatassannihitadeśa iva dūradeśābhimato 'pi śabdaḥ śrūyeta / na vānyo 'pītyekāntaḥ / dikkālayoścaikatvāt pūrvāparādipratyayānupapattiḥ / etena nityasyāpi manaso 'sambhava eva / tathā hi - yugapajjñānānutpattyā mano 'numīyate tadvādibhiḥ / anubhūyanta eva yugapadbahūni jñānāni narttakīdarśanādau / yadi punarmano [nityaṃ] syāttadānīmetāni jñānāni na yujyante / tasmānnāstyeva mano 'pi //
body.translated_text: Now, is there something real called <s>ākāśa</s> (space), or is there not? There is not. For where there is tangible substance (<s>sapratigha dravya</s>), space does not provide room there. Where there is no [substance], room is already established by the very absence of that [substance] — so where would space provide room? [Since space is said to be that which provides room,] therefore, if it existed, there would always be room everywhere in every way. But this is not the case. Therefore we maintain that space simply does not exist. This refutation has been stated with reference to the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> view. Others, however, hold that <s>ākāśa</s> has sound as its quality. If that [space] is one, then because of occupying the same location, one could not hear different sounds distinctly — and then a sound intended for a distant place would also be heard just as at a proximate location. Nor is there any definitive alternative. And since direction (<s>dik</s>) and time (<s>kāla</s>) would [also] be one, the cognitions of 'before,' 'after,' and the like would be inexplicable. By this same reasoning, a permanent mind (<s>manas</s>) is also impossible. For the proponents of mind infer it from the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions. But in fact, many cognitions are experienced simultaneously, as in watching a dancer. Moreover, if mind were permanent, then these cognitions would not be possible. Therefore, mind too simply does not exist.

body.text: avayavinirasanapūrvakaṃ paramāṇumātrasamarthanam
body.translated_text: Establishing atoms alone, preceded by the refutation of wholes (<s>avayavin</s>)

body.text: pṛthivyādayo 'vaśiṣyante / te cāvayaviparamāṇubhedena dvidhā iṣyante / tatra yo 'vayavī ghaṭādiḥ paramāṇubhidvaryaṇukādi krameṇārabdhaḥ prasiddhaḥ, tasya upalabdhi lakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalambho bādhaka ityuktam / yadyavayavī nāsti kathaṃ tarhyayamekatvena pratibhāsata iti cet -
body.translated_text: Earth and the other [elements] remain [to be discussed]. They are held to be of two kinds: wholes (<s>avayavin</s>) and atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>). The well-known whole, such as a pot, which is successively produced from atoms through dyads (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>) and triads, etc. — it has been stated that non-apprehension of what fulfills the conditions for apprehension is a defeating proof [against its existence]. If a whole does not exist, then how does this appear as a unity? —

children.translated_text: It is only the parts that appear, arranged in such and such a way;
but no partless whole whatsoever is ever cognized.

body.text: ityuktam / nanu ko 'yaṃ bhāgapratibhāso nāma? nānādigdeśāvaṣṣṭambhena sañcitaḥ paramāṇupratibhāsa eva / yadyevaṃ kathaṃ 'pratibhāsadharmaḥ sthaulyam' ityuktaṃ dharmottareṇa,tatrāpyayamevārthaḥ arthasya svarūpeṇa nāsti vedanam, 'bhāktaṃ syādarthavedanam' iti vacanāt / tasmādyo 'yaṃ nīlādiprabhāso nānādeśavyāpitvenānubhūyate sa eva sthūlapratibhāsa ityadoṣaḥ ye 'pi tadārambhakāḥ paramāṇavo vaiśeṣikāṇāṃ, sākṣādadhyakṣyagocarā vaibhāṣikāṇāṃ darśane, svasvākārasamarpaṇapravaṇāḥ sautrāntikānāṃ mate, te 'pi yogācārāṇāṃ darśane na sambhavanti / na khalvekaḥ paramāṇuḥ prasiddhimadhyāste / tasyādharottaracaturdikṣu paramāṇumadhyāsīnasya niyamena ṣaḍaṃśatāpatteḥ / yo hyasya svabhāvaḥ pūrvaparamāṇupratyāsannaḥ na sa evāparaparamāṇupratyāsanno ghaṭate / tayorekadeśatāprāpteḥ / evaṃ ca sa pūrvaparamāṇusannihitasvabhāvo 'paraparamāṇuṃ pratyāsīdedyadi so 'pi tatra syāt / asatyāmapi pratyāsattāvābhimukhyamātre 'pyayameva vṛttāntaḥ / tataśca paramāṇumātraṃ piṇḍaḥ prasaktaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus it has been stated. Now, what is this so-called appearance of parts? It is precisely the appearance of atoms, assembled by being stationed in various directions and locations. If so, how did <s>Dharmottara</s> state that 'grossness is a property of appearance'? Even there, the meaning is just this: there is no cognition of an object in its own form, since it is said that 'cognition of objects is figurative (<s>bhākta</s>).' Therefore, this very appearance of blue and the like, experienced as pervading various locations, is the gross appearance — and there is no fault. As for the atoms that compose [these wholes] — according to the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>, they are directly perceptible objects; in the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> view, they are objects of immediate sensory cognition; and in the <s>Sautrāntika</s> view, they are disposed to impart their own respective forms [to cognition]. But even these are impossible according to the <s>Yogācāra</s> view. Indeed, no single atom can maintain its identity. For an atom situated amidst [other] atoms in the four cardinal directions, above and below, necessarily incurs the consequence of having six parts. For the nature of it that is proximate to the eastern atom cannot be the very same as that which is proximate to the western atom, since that would entail their being in the same location. And thus, if [an atom] with its nature proximate to the eastern atom were to approach the western atom, then that [eastern atom] too would be there [in the same location]. Even without actual proximity, with mere facing alone, this same situation applies. Consequently, the absurd consequence follows that a mass would be merely atom-sized.

body.text: yogācārasya matam
body.translated_text: The view of the <s>Yogācāra</s>

body.text: athavāyaṃ vicāraḥ, yadetatpratibhāsamānaṃ tadekaṃ tāvanna yuktam, anantaroktavicārāt / nāpyanekaṃ, paramāṇuśaḥ paramāṇorayogāt / tathā hi - yadyasau sāṃśaḥ kathaṃ paramāṇuḥ? atha niraṃśaḥ tadā saṃyuktāḥ paramāṇāvaḥ sarvātmanā saṃyogāt parasparamabhinnadeśāḥ syuriti sarvaḥ piṇḍaḥ paramāṇumātraṃ syāt, parvato 'pi kṣitirapīti / tasmādavaśyaṃ tayoḥ svabhāvayorbhedo 'bhyupetavyaḥ / yathā cānayostathā
body.translated_text: Alternatively, here is the analysis: that which appears — first, it cannot logically be one, due to the analysis just stated. Nor can it be many, atom by atom, because atoms are untenable. For if [an atom] has parts, how is it an atom? And if it is partless, then atoms in conjunction, being in contact with their entire being, would occupy the same location as each other — thus every mass would be merely atom-sized, even a mountain, even the earth. Therefore, a difference between the natures of those two [atoms in contact] must necessarily be acknowledged. And just as between these two, so also

body.text: `dharottaradakṣiṇottaraparamāṇupratyāsannānāṃ svabhābānāṃ ca bheda iti ṣaḍaṃśataiva paramāṇornyāyabalādāpatati / yadāha -
body.translated_text: between the natures proximate to the atoms below, above, to the south, and to the north — there is difference; thus the six-partedness of an atom inevitably follows by force of reasoning. As it is said —

children.translated_text: Due to simultaneous contact with six [atoms], the atom has six parts;
due to the six occupying the same location, a mass would be merely atom-sized.

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: na caikāsiddhau anekasyāpi siddhiriti na santi paramāṇavaḥ / yadi bāhyo 'rtho nāsti kiṃ viṣayastarhyayaṃ pratibhāsaḥ? pratibhāsaḥ khalveṣo 'nādivitathavāsanātaḥ pravartamāno nirālambana eva lakṣyate / tathā hi - sati viṣaye sālambanatā syāt / tena cāvayavinā bhavitavyam, paramāṇupracayena vā / sa cāyamubhayo 'pyanantarokta bādhakapramāṇa [grāha] grastavigraho na vyomatāmarasamatiśete yathoktam -
body.translated_text: And since, when the one [atom] is not established, the many cannot be established either — therefore atoms do not exist. If external objects do not exist, then what is the object of this appearance? This appearance, proceeding from beginningless false impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), is seen to be without any support (<s>nirālambana</s>). For if there were an [external] object, it would have a support. And that [object] would have to be either a whole (<s>avayavin</s>) or an aggregate of atoms. But both of these, their positions consumed by the defeating proofs just stated, do not surpass the status of sky-flowers. As it is said —

body.text: na sannāvayavī nāma na santi paramāṇavaḥ /
body.translated_text:
There is no whole whatsoever, nor do atoms exist;
appearance is without support, like the experience in a dream.

body.text: pratibhāso nirālambhaḥ svapnānubhavasannibhaḥ // iti //
nirālambanavādaḥ
body.translated_text: The doctrine of absence of support (<s>nirālambana-vāda</s>)

body.text: svapnajñānaṃ nirālambanaṃ viditameva / na ca svaprajāgradanubhavayorbhedaḥ kaścidapyasti / sarvaprakārasādharmyadarśanāt / na cānālambanādanavāptarūpaviśeṣaṃ vijñānaṃ sālambanasambandhamanubhavitumutsahate / yadanālambanādaviśiṣṭaṃ tadanālambanam, yathaikasmādākāśakeśadarśanāt dvitīyam [jñānaṃ] anālambanācca svapnajñānādaviśiṣṭaṃ vivādāspadībhūtaṃ jāgradvijñānamiti svabhāvahetuḥ //
body.translated_text: Dream cognition is known to be without support. And there is no difference whatsoever between dream and waking experience, since complete similarity in every respect is observed. And a cognition that has not acquired a distinctive form from a supportless [cognition] cannot be said to have a connection with a supported [object]. Whatever is indistinguishable from what is without support is itself without support — just as from one instance of seeing hair-like lines in the sky, a second [cognition is inferred to be without support]. And waking cognition, which is the point of dispute, is indistinguishable from the supportless dream cognition — thus [this is] an inference from essential nature (<s>svabhāva-hetu</s>).

body.text: vijñānasyasya sākāratvanirākāratvapakṣabhedaḥ
body.translated_text: The distinction between the positions of cognition being with-form (<s>sākāra</s>) and without-form (<s>nirākāra</s>)

body.text: yadi bāhyo 'rtho nāsti kiṃ tarhi paramārthasat? grāhyagrāhakādikalaṅkānaṅkitaṃ niṣprapañcavijñānamātraṃ paramārthasat / yathoktam -
body.translated_text: If external objects do not exist, then what is ultimately real (<s>paramārthasat</s>)? Pure cognition alone (<s>vijñānamātra</s>), free from the stains of apprehended and apprehender (<s>grāhya-grāhaka</s>) and the like, free from conceptual elaboration (<s>niṣprapañca</s>), is ultimately real. As it is said —

body.text: `grāhyagrāhakanirmuktaṃ vijñānaṃ paramārthasat' iti /
body.translated_text: 'Cognition free from apprehended and apprehender is ultimately real.'

body.text: punaścoktam -
body.translated_text: And further it is said —

children.translated_text: 'There is nothing to be experienced apart from cognition, nor is there any other experience of it;
due to the absence of apprehended and apprehender, it itself illuminates itself.'

body.text: `uktaṃ caitadbhagavatā -
body.translated_text: And this was stated by the Blessed One (<s>Bhagavat</s>) —

children.translated_text: 'External objects do not truly exist as they are imagined by the childish;
the mind, agitated by impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), operates with the appearance of objects.'

body.text: sākāravādināṃ matam
body.translated_text: The view of the proponents of cognition with-form (<s>sākāra-vādin</s>)

body.text: tatra kecidevamāhuḥ - vijñānamevedaṃ sarva sarvaśarīraviṣayabhāvena prasiddham, tacca svasaṃvedanamiti na kasyacit grāhyaṃ grāhakaṃ vā / kalpanayā tu grāhyagrāhakabhāva iti vyavasthāpyate / tataḥ parikalpitagrāhyagrāhakabhāvarahitaṃ vijñānaṃ [sākāraṃ] satyamiti /
body.translated_text: Among them, some say thus: all this is nothing but cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>), manifesting in the form of all bodies and objects; and that is self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>), so it is neither apprehended nor apprehender for anyone. But through conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>), the distinction of apprehended and apprehender is established. Therefore, cognition that is free from the conceptually constructed distinction of apprehended and apprehender is true [and has form (<s>sākāra</s>)].

body.text: nirākāravādināṃ matam
body.translated_text: The view of the proponents of cognition without-form (<s>nirākāra-vādin</s>)

body.text: anye tu sakalākārakalaṅkānaṅkitaṃ śuddhasphaṭikasaṃkāśaṃ vāstavaṃ vijñānam / ākārāstvamī vitathā evāvidyayā darśitāḥ prakāśante / tasmāt grāhyaṃ nāma nāstyeva grāhyābhāvāt tadapekṣayā yadgrāhakatvaṃ vijñānasya tadapi nāstīti / mādhyamikānāṃ tu darśane tadapi vijñānaṃ na paramārthasat, vicārāsahatvāt / svabhāvena hi yuktaṃ pāramārthika mucyate loke / na cāsya vicārataḥ kaścitsvabhāvo ghaṭate, eko vāneko vā, pūrvavicārāsahatvāt / yathoktam - 'neṣṭaṃ tadapi dhīrāṇā vijñānaṃ pāramārthikam / ekānekasvabhāvena viyogādganābjavat' // iti //
body.translated_text: Others, however, [hold that] real consciousness — unstained by the blemish of any form whatsoever, resembling pure crystal — [is ultimately real]. The forms are entirely false, made to appear by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). Therefore, the graspable (<s>grāhya</s>) simply does not exist; and because of the absence of the graspable, the grasper-nature (<s>grāhakatva</s>) of consciousness also does not exist. But according to the <s>Mādhyamika</s> view, even that consciousness is not ultimately real (<s>paramārthasat</s>), because it cannot withstand critical examination. For what is endowed with own-nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) is called ultimately [real] in the world. And no own-nature of this [consciousness] is tenable upon examination — whether one or many — because it cannot withstand the earlier examination. As it has been said: 'The wise do not accept even consciousness as ultimately real; because it is devoid of the nature of being one or many, like a sky-lotus.' Thus.

body.text: kīrtipādairapyuktam -
body.translated_text: As has also been said by <s>Kīrtipāda</s> —

children.translated_text: 'The nature by which entities are examined does not exist in reality;

children.text: yasmādekamanekaṃ vā rūpaṃ teṣu na vidyate' // iti //
children.translated_text: because neither a single nor a manifold nature is found in them.' Thus.

body.text: tathālaṅkārakāreṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: Likewise, it has been said by the author of the <s>Alaṅkāra</s> (Ornament) —

children.text: `yadā tu na vikalpasya na cānyasya pramāṇatā /
children.translated_text: 'When neither conceptual construction nor anything else has validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition),
then even when everything is crumbling, who is at fault?'
'The distinction of bound and liberated and so forth does not exist in ultimate reality (<s>paramārthatas</s>);
for distinction does not appear at all to those who see equally everywhere.' Thus.

body.text: prayogaḥ punarevam - yadekānekasvabhāvaṃ na bhavati na tatparamārthasat, yathā vyomakamalam,ekānekasvabhāvaṃ ca na bhavati vijñānamiti vyāpakānupalabdhiḥ / na tāvadayamasiddho hetuḥ / sākāre jñāne bahirartha iva ekānesvabhāvāyogyatvasya parisphuṭatvāt / yatra hi lokasya bāhyārthavyavahārastadeva sākāravādino jñānam, tato yattasya bahirbhāve bādhakaṃ tadevāntarbhāve 'pi bādhakam / na hi sthūlamekamanekaṃ ca paramāṇurūpamapīṣyate / vijñānātmakānāmayamākāro yadyekaḥ sthūlo yati vānekaḥ paramāṇuśo bhinnaḥ, ubhayathāpi bāhyārthapakṣabhāvi dūṣaṇamaśakyamurddhatum / na hi tadvijñāne bahirbhāvanibandhanaṃ dūṣaṇam! yena tadbhāvena bhavet / mūrtinimittaṃ bādhakam,
body.translated_text: The formal proof is as follows: whatever does not have the nature of being one or many is not ultimately real, like a sky-lotus (<s>vyomakamala</s>). And consciousness does not have the nature of being one or many — this is non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>). Now, this reason is not unestablished. Because in the <s>sākāra</s> (with-form) cognition, the unfitness for being one or many is clearly evident, just as for the external object. For whatever the common person treats as an external object is precisely the cognition for the <s>sākāravādin</s> (proponent of the with-form view). Hence, whatever refutes the externality of that [object] also refutes its internality. For neither the gross [object as] one, nor the atomic form [as] many, is accepted [as ultimately real]. If this form, being of the nature of consciousness, is one and gross, or many and divided atom by atom — in either case, the defect that applies to the external-object position cannot be surmounted. For that defect in cognition is not dependent on externality, such that it would arise [only] with externality. [The objection that] the refutation applies [only] to what is material,

body.text: nāmūrte vijñānātmani ityapi nissāram / sākāratāyāṃ vijñānasyāpi mūrtatvāt / ayameva hi deśāvitānavā [nākāro] mūrtiriti // śrīmanmahājagaddalavihārīya mahāpaṇḍita bhikṣumokṣākaraguptaviracitāyāṃ tarkabhāṣāyaṃ parārthānumānaparicchedaḥ tṛtīyaḥ samāptaḥ //
body.translated_text: and not to consciousness, which is immaterial — this too is groundless, because when consciousness has forms (<s>sākāratā</s>), it too is material. For this very spatial extension [of the form] is materiality (<s>mūrti</s>). — In the <s>Tarkabhāṣā</s> composed by the great <s>paṇḍita</s>, <s>Bhikṣu</s> <s>Mokṣākaragupta</s> of the illustrious great <s>Jagaddala</s> monastery, the third chapter on inference for others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) is completed.

body.translated_text: The extent of the treatise in verse-measure (<s>ślokamāna</s>): 840.

children.translated_text: Having composed this <s>Tarkabhāṣā</s>, whatever merit has been obtained by me,
by that merit, may this world attain <s>Buddhahood</s>.

children.text: * yādṛśaṃ pustake dṛṣṭaṃ tādṛśaṃ likhitaṃ mayā /
children.translated_text: * As it was seen in the manuscript, so it has been written by me;

children.text: yadi śuddhamaśuddhaṃ vā mama doṣo na dīyate //
children.translated_text: whether correct or incorrect, no fault should be attributed to me.
From water, fire, thieves, and foolish persons alike,
the scripture written with great effort should be carefully preserved. *

body.translated_text: The <s>Tarkabhāṣā</s> is completed.
